# The Google Meet Transcript Nobody Can Find

*This story was written with AI assistance and edited by the Lynkk team.*

Ask a room of Google Workspace users where their meeting transcripts live and you get three answers: "in Drive somewhere," "in the calendar event, I think," and "wait, we have transcripts?"

All three are partly right. That is the problem.

Google Meet can produce a transcript, and on the plans that include it, the feature works. The file is not really where things go wrong. Things go wrong in the gap between a transcript existing and anyone using it.

## A transcript is a file, not a memory

When transcription is on, Meet writes a Google Doc and saves it to the organizer's Drive, usually in a "Meet Recordings" folder. It also links the doc from the calendar event. The organizer gets an email when it is ready.

Look at who that serves. The organizer gets the file. Everyone else gets a link inside a calendar event they will never open again. If the organizer leaves the company, the doc goes wherever their Drive goes.

Now think about how people actually look for information after a meeting. Nobody wants "the transcript of the Tuesday sync." They want to know whether Priya agreed to the 28th, or what the customer said about their budget. A transcript answers that only if you can find the right doc, open it and scroll through forty minutes of text.

So the first lesson is simple. **A transcript you have to go and find is a file. A transcript you can ask a question of is a memory.** Most teams have files.

If you just need the mechanics of finding, downloading and fixing Meet transcripts, our team keeps a step-by-step [Google Meet transcript guide](https://lynkk.ai/blog/google-meet-transcript). It covers which Workspace plans include transcripts, where the doc is saved, and what to do when the button is greyed out.

## Three reasons the transcript goes missing

Teams lose Meet transcripts for boring, repeatable reasons.

**1. Nobody pressed the button.** On most setups, someone has to start transcription in each meeting. In a back-to-back day, "someone" quickly becomes "nobody." Recurring meetings are the worst offenders, because everyone assumes someone else turned it on.

**2. The wrong person owns it.** The transcript belongs to the organizer. In a cross-team meeting, that might be a coordinator who wasn't even in the room for the part that mattered.

**3. The plan doesn't include it.** Transcription depends on your Workspace edition. A team on a plan without it can spend weeks thinking the feature is broken.

None of these failures is a technology problem. They are ownership problems, and ownership problems come back unless you design them out.

## What a "found" transcript looks like

Picture a 12-person product team that meets on Google Meet all day. Imagine their transcripts actually work for them. What is different?

- **Capture is automatic.** Nobody has to remember to start it. Either the meeting tool does it by policy, or a note taker joins from the calendar.
- **Output is short first.** People read a summary with decisions and action items. The full transcript is one click away for when they need the exact words.
- **Owners and dates come out of the call.** An action item without an owner is a wish. A good summary names who and by when.
- **Everything is searchable in one place.** Not across thirty organizers' Drives.

That third point is where most teams stop short. A transcript tells you what was said. It does not tell you what happens next. Writing that part down takes about ten minutes after each call, and a [meeting summary template](https://lynkk.ai/blog/meeting-summary-template) with fixed sections (decisions, action items, open questions) makes those ten minutes predictable.

## Native transcripts vs a note taker

There is a fair question here: if Google already transcribes, why add anything?

Often you shouldn't. If your team meets only on Meet, your plan includes transcripts and Gemini's notes, and people actually read them, you may be fine. Do not buy a tool to fix a habit you could fix with a calendar reminder.

A separate note taker starts to earn its place when:

- you also meet on Zoom or Teams, or in person, and want one archive instead of three;
- people speak more than one language in the same call;
- you want the action items to go somewhere, like a Jira project, rather than sit in a doc;
- you want to ask questions across months of meetings, not just read one.

We wrote a longer comparison of [AI note takers for Google Meet](https://lynkk.ai/blog/google-meet-ai-note-taker), including Gemini's own notes, if you want to weigh the options without a sales pitch.

## A 10-minute fix you can make this week

Before you change any tools, try this with your team:

1. **Pick one recurring meeting** that keeps producing "wait, what did we decide?" moments.
2. **Make transcription automatic** for that meeting, or assign a named owner for capture. Not "whoever remembers."
3. **Send a five-line summary within the hour**: the decisions, the action items with owners and dates, and one open question.
4. **Put every summary in the same place**, a shared folder or channel, never someone's personal Drive.
5. **After two weeks, ask the team** whether they used any of it. Be honest about the answer.

If the answer is yes, you've learned that capture was the bottleneck, and you can automate it. If the answer is no, the problem was never the transcript. It was that the meeting didn't need one.

Either way, you'll stop asking where the transcript went.

# Your Meeting Notes Are Not Your Minutes (and Neither Is Your Memory)

*This story was written with AI assistance and edited by the Lynkk team.*

Every organization keeps some record of its meetings. Very few can say what that record is for.

That sounds pedantic until you watch what happens. A board asks to see the minutes and gets someone's bullet points. A new hire asks why a decision was made and gets a link to a 50-minute recording. A manager writes beautiful notes that nobody but the manager ever reads.

The fix starts with a distinction most people skip. There are three different records a meeting can leave behind, and each one has a different job.

## Record 1: Notes are for the people in the room

Meeting notes are working material. They are informal, often personal, and written to help the people who were there remember and act.

Good notes are short. They capture:

- what was decided,
- who is doing what, and by when,
- what is still open.

Notes don't need to be complete. They need to be useful by tomorrow morning. If you have to read your notes twice to work out what you're supposed to do, they failed.

## Record 2: Minutes are for the people who weren't

Minutes are a formal record. Boards, committees, nonprofits, school councils and regulated businesses keep them because someone outside the meeting (an auditor, a member, a court, a future board) may need to rely on them.

That changes what goes in. Minutes record who attended, whether there was a quorum, the motions made, who moved and seconded them, and how the vote went. They are approved at the next meeting. They usually *don't* record every argument, and in many organizations they shouldn't.

The most common mistake is treating minutes like long notes. They aren't. They are closer to a legal summary of actions taken. If you've never written them, it helps to start from a real [meeting minutes sample](https://lynkk.ai/blog/meeting-minutes-sample) rather than a blank page.

For the full side-by-side, including why they're called minutes at all, the Lynkk team wrote a guide to [meeting notes vs minutes](https://lynkk.ai/blog/meeting-notes-vs-minutes) and how to turn one into the other.

## Record 3: Memory is for the team six months from now

Here's the record almost nobody keeps on purpose.

Six months after a meeting, nobody needs the notes or the minutes. They need an answer:

- "Why did we drop the annual plan?"
- "What did the customer say about their security review?"
- "Did we ever agree on a launch date with marketing?"

Notes are too scattered to answer that. Minutes are too formal. Recordings are too long. What you need is the ability to search across many meetings and get an answer with a pointer to where it was said.

This is what people mean when they talk about "knowledge management" for meetings. It's less about software than about one property: **can someone who wasn't there find the reason for a decision without asking the person who was?** If not, your team's memory sits in people's heads, and it leaves when they do.

We've written about the [tools teams use to turn meetings into searchable memory](https://lynkk.ai/blog/meeting-knowledge-management), from wikis to AI search with cited answers.

## Why one record can't do all three jobs

Teams usually pick one of these and stretch it.

**Notes stretched into minutes** miss the formal parts (attendance, motions, votes) and include things that shouldn't be in a permanent record.

**Minutes stretched into notes** are too slow. By the time they're approved, the action items are a week old.

**Recordings stretched into memory** technically contain everything and practically contain nothing, because no one will scrub through them.

Each record has a different reader, a different deadline and a different level of formality:

| Record | Reader | Deadline | Formality |
|---|---|---|---|
| Notes | People in the room | Within hours | Low |
| Minutes | People who weren't there, plus auditors | Next meeting | High |
| Memory | The team, months later | Whenever the question comes up | Searchable, cited |

## A simple setup that covers all three

You don't need a new system. You need each record to have an owner and a default.

1. **Notes: automatic by default.** Capture the call (by hand or with a note taker) and send a short summary with decisions and owners the same day.
2. **Minutes: only where they're required.** For a board or committee, one named person drafts minutes from the notes using a fixed template, and the group approves them at the next meeting.
3. **Memory: one searchable place.** Every set of notes goes into the same archive. Not ten personal folders. If your tool can answer questions across meetings and show the source, use it. If not, a shared, consistently named folder is a fine start.

The test is the six-month question. Pick a decision your team made last quarter and try to find out why it was made, without asking anyone. How long did it take?

If the answer is "I gave up," you don't have a notes problem. You have a memory problem.

# Action Items Die in the Chat. Here Are 5 Rules That Keep Them Alive.

*This story was written with AI assistance and edited by the Lynkk team.*

There's a moment near the end of most meetings when someone says, "Great, so we'll follow up on that." Everyone nods. The call ends. And the follow-up quietly dies in a chat thread nobody scrolls back to.

It isn't laziness. Most action items fail for structural reasons, which is good news, because structural problems have structural fixes.

Here are five rules. None of them needs new software. All of them work better with it.

## Rule 1: An action item has exactly one owner

"Marketing will look into it" is not an action item. Neither is "we should." When a task belongs to a team, it belongs to nobody.

Write a name. One name. If two people truly share the work, one of them still owns making sure it happens.

This one change fixes more follow-through problems than any tool. If you only adopt one rule, adopt this one.

## Rule 2: It starts with a verb and ends with a date

Compare:

- "Pricing page"
- "Dana to send the revised pricing page draft to Sam by Thursday"

The first is a topic. The second is a commitment. A useful action item answers three questions: **who** does **what** by **when**.

If nobody can name a date, ask why. Usually the honest answer is "we haven't decided whether to do it," which means it's an open question, not an action item. Write it down as one.

There's a longer list of [action item examples and a copyable template](https://lynkk.ai/blog/action-items-examples-template) on the Lynkk blog, if you want to see good and bad versions side by side.

## Rule 3: Capture them in the meeting, not after

Memory decays fast. If you rebuild the list from memory an hour later, you'll get the big items and lose the small ones, and the small ones are usually what blocks the big ones.

Two ways to do this:

1. **Assign a scribe** whose only job is to write down decisions and action items as they're said, and read them back in the last two minutes.
2. **Record the call** and let a note taker pull out the action items, then spend the last two minutes confirming them out loud.

Either way, the read-back is the important part. "Here's what I have, is anything missing or wrong?" catches most mistakes while everyone is still in the room.

## Rule 4: Send them where the work already lives

This is where most teams lose. The action items are written down, and then they live in a Google Doc, a Notion page or a chat message, which is to say nowhere anyone looks on a Tuesday.

Action items should land in the place where that kind of work is tracked:

- engineering tasks in Jira or your issue tracker;
- customer commitments in the CRM or the account plan;
- personal follow-ups in the owner's own task list.

For product and engineering teams, sending action items straight into Jira closes the loop. We wrote up [how teams turn meeting minutes into Jira issues](https://lynkk.ai/blog/meeting-minutes-to-jira), including what to put in the issue so it still makes sense to someone who wasn't on the call.

## Rule 5: Close the loop in writing within 24 hours

The follow-up message is where an agreement becomes official. Without it, everyone leaves with a slightly different memory of what was decided.

Keep it short:

> **Decided:** We'll launch the pilot with 15 users on the 28th.
> **Action items:**
> Dana: revised pricing draft to Sam, Thursday.
> Dev: QA sign-off on the pilot build, Friday.
> **Open:** Who owns the customer training session?

That's it. Five lines. Send it to everyone who attended, plus anyone who owns an item but wasn't there. If you send these to clients or prospects, the tone matters more; there are [12 follow-up email examples](https://lynkk.ai/blog/follow-up-email-after-meeting) for different situations if you need a starting point.

## Why the chat thread is the worst place for action items

It's tempting to post the follow-up in the team chat and call it done. The trouble is that chat is designed to move. Today's action items get buried by tomorrow's jokes, and nobody can check off a chat message.

Use chat to *announce* the follow-up. Use your task tracker to *hold* it.

## The two-week test

Here's how to tell whether your action items are working. Take any meeting from two weeks ago and ask:

1. Can I find the list of action items in under a minute?
2. Does every item have one owner and a date?
3. How many are done?

If you can't answer the first question, start with Rule 4. If you can't answer the second, start with Rules 1 and 2. If the third answer is "almost none," the meeting probably agreed to things nobody actually intended to do, and that's a conversation worth having in the next meeting.

# Typing Is the Bottleneck. What Voice-to-Text Actually Fixes, and What It Doesn't.

*This story was written with AI assistance and edited by the Lynkk team.*

Most people speak far faster than they type. That gap is the whole pitch for voice-to-text: talk, and the words appear.

It's a good pitch, and for some work it's completely true. For other work it makes things worse. The difference has less to do with which app you pick than with what kind of writing you're doing.

## Where dictation genuinely wins

**First drafts.** The hardest part of writing is getting something down. Speaking lowers the bar. You ramble, you repeat yourself, and then you have 600 words to edit instead of a blinking cursor.

**Replies you've been avoiding.** That email you've been putting off for three days takes ninety seconds to say out loud. Editing it takes another two minutes.

**Notes right after a conversation.** Walking out of a meeting and saying "Okay, three things: Sam owns the pricing draft, the customer wants a case study, and we never agreed on the launch date" is faster and more complete than typing it later.

**Anyone whose hands are the problem.** Repetitive strain, injury, or just a long day. Dictation isn't a productivity trick here; it's an accessibility tool, and a good one.

## Where dictation loses

**Precise editing.** Changing one word in the middle of a sentence by voice is slower than reaching for the mouse. Most people end up dictating and then editing with the keyboard, which is the right split.

**Code and structured text.** Variable names, punctuation-heavy syntax and tables are painful to speak. There are tools for voice coding, but they take real practice.

**Open-plan offices.** Nobody wants to hear you dictate your performance review.

**Thinking on the page.** Some writing is a way of figuring out what you think. If you need to stare at a sentence and rearrange it, speaking won't help.

## You probably already own a good dictation tool

Before buying anything, try the free one on your device:

- **Mac:** Dictation is built in. Press the dictation key (or Fn twice, depending on your settings) in almost any text field. Our guide to [dictation on Mac](https://lynkk.ai/blog/dictation-on-mac) covers turning it on and six fixes for when it stops working.
- **Windows:** Press Windows key + H to start voice typing in most apps.
- **Google Docs:** Tools, then Voice typing, in Chrome.
- **Microsoft Word:** The Dictate button on the Home tab, for Microsoft 365 users. Here's how to [dictate in Microsoft Word](https://lynkk.ai/blog/dictate-in-microsoft-word), including the voice commands for punctuation and new lines.

For many people that's enough. The built-in tools have improved a lot, and they cost nothing.

## When a paid app is worth it

Free dictation tends to fall short in the same few places:

1. **It's tied to one app or one browser.** You want it everywhere, including in Slack, your email client and your notes app.
2. **It doesn't clean up.** You get "um, so, the, the thing is" verbatim. Better tools remove filler words and fix punctuation.
3. **It struggles with your vocabulary.** Product names, client names, medical or legal terms. A custom dictionary helps a lot.
4. **It handles one language at a time.** If you switch between, say, Hindi and English in the same sentence, many tools fall apart.

If two or more of those describe your day, a dedicated app is worth trying. The Lynkk team compared [7 voice-to-text apps](https://lynkk.ai/blog/voice-to-text-apps), from Apple Dictation and Windows voice typing to Dragon, on what each does well and what it costs.

## A simple way to start

Don't try to dictate everything. Try this for one week:

1. **Pick one kind of writing**: email replies, meeting notes or first drafts. Just one.
2. **Dictate the draft, edit with the keyboard.** Don't try to fix mistakes by voice.
3. **Speak in full sentences and say the punctuation** ("comma", "period", "new paragraph") until the tool learns your rhythm.
4. **Keep a list of words it gets wrong**, then add them to the custom dictionary if your tool has one.

At the end of the week, compare how long that kind of writing took. If it saved time, add a second kind. If it didn't, you've lost nothing but a week of slightly odd emails.

## The honest summary

Voice-to-text is a first-draft machine. It's excellent at getting words out of your head and bad at polishing them. Use it to start, use the keyboard to finish, and you'll get most of the speed with none of the frustration.

---

# The 15-Minute Standup Nobody Remembers by Lunch

*This story was written with AI assistance and edited by the Lynkk team.*

Here's a question people actually type into search engines: *"Our daily standups run 15 minutes and by afternoon nobody remembers what was said. How do teams keep a record without someone typing?"*

It's a good question, because it names the trade-off at the heart of every standup. The meeting is short so it doesn't eat the day. Because it's short, nobody writes anything down. Because nobody writes anything down, the one useful sentence ("I'm blocked on the API key from the platform team") is gone by 2 p.m.

## What a standup is actually for

Strip away the ritual and a standup has one job: **surface blockers early enough that someone can remove them today.**

Status updates are a side effect. If everyone already knows what everyone else is doing (from the board, from the pull requests), the status part can shrink to almost nothing. The blocker part can't.

That means the record you need from a standup is small. You don't need minutes. You need three things:

1. the blockers, with who can unblock them;
2. any decision made on the spot ("we'll ship without the export for now");
3. any new task that came out of it, with an owner.

Everything else can evaporate, and that's fine.

## Why nobody writes it down

Three reasons, all reasonable:

- **The facilitator is facilitating.** Running the meeting and taking notes at the same time is hard, and the notes lose.
- **Rotating scribes get rusty.** The person on scribe duty this week writes half as much as last week's.
- **It feels like overkill.** Writing notes for a 15-minute meeting seems like bureaucracy, right up until the day someone asks "didn't Dev say he was blocked on this last week?"

## Four ways teams keep a record (from lightest to heaviest)

**1. Blockers go on the board, live.** When someone says they're blocked, the facilitator adds a "blocked" label or a comment on the ticket during the standup. No separate notes at all. This works well for teams that already live in Jira or Linear.

**2. A three-line post in chat.** Right after the call, one person posts: blockers, decisions, new tasks. It takes two minutes. The weakness is that chat scrolls away, so link it to the board when it matters.

**3. Async standups.** Everyone writes their update in a thread before a set time, and the live meeting (if there is one) is only for blockers. This gives you a written record for free, at the cost of some human contact.

**4. Record it and let a note taker summarize.** The call is captured automatically, and a summary with blockers and action items arrives a few minutes later. Nobody types. The cost is that people need to be comfortable being recorded, so ask, and tell the team where the recordings go.

There's no single right answer. A co-located team with a strong board culture may never need more than option 1. A distributed team across time zones may find option 3 or 4 essential.

## A standup format that's easy to capture

Whatever method you pick, the format of the standup itself makes capture easier or harder. Here's a format that produces a clean record almost by accident:

- **Walk the board, not the people.** Go column by column, right to left (closest to done first). Blockers come up naturally.
- **Say "blocker" out loud.** Make it a keyword. Anyone capturing notes, human or software, knows to write down what comes next.
- **Park discussions.** Anything that takes longer than a minute gets a name and a time ("Dana and Sam, after standup") and becomes its own action item.
- **End with a 30-second read-back.** "Blockers: one. API key, Priya owns. New task: Dev to spike the export." Done.

For a fuller template, including what to say and how long it should last, the Lynkk team wrote a guide to [running a standup meeting with an agenda and AI notes](https://lynkk.ai/blog/daily-standup-meeting).

## The blocker is an action item in disguise

The most useful mental shift: a blocker is just an action item for someone else. "I'm blocked on the API key" becomes "Priya to send Dev the staging API key by noon."

Once you write it that way, it gets an owner and a time, and it stops being a complaint and starts being a commitment. The same rules that make any action item work (one owner, a verb, a date) apply here too. There are [examples of well-written action items](https://lynkk.ai/blog/action-items-examples-template) if you want to calibrate.

## Try it for two weeks

Pick one of the four capture methods. Use the board-walking format. End every standup with the read-back.

After two weeks, check one thing: when someone asks "wasn't this blocked last week?", can you answer in under a minute?

If yes, you've solved the problem the searcher above was asking about. If you want to remove the typing entirely, that's where recording helps; here's how [teams use Lynkk for standups](https://lynkk.ai/use-cases/team-standups) without anyone taking notes.

# Founders Are the Company's Hard Drive. That's a Problem.

*This story was written with AI assistance and edited by the Lynkk team.*

In the first year of a startup, founders are in every important conversation. Every customer call, every investor meeting, every hiring decision. That's not a flaw. It's how small companies move fast.

The trouble starts later, usually somewhere between 15 and 40 people. The founders are still in most of those conversations, but now there are a dozen people who need what was said in them. And the only place it's stored is the founders' memory.

One search query sums it up better than we can: *"We're about 30 people and all the context from customer and investor calls lives in the founders' heads. How do we get it out without adding process?"*

## The cost of the founder hard drive

It doesn't feel like a problem, because the founders can always answer the question. That's exactly why it's expensive.

- **Every answer costs founder time.** "What did Acme say about pricing?" is a two-minute Slack message, twenty times a day.
- **Answers get compressed.** By the time a customer's words pass through a founder's summary, the nuance is gone. "They're keen" can mean anything.
- **Things get lost when founders are busy.** A promise made on a Tuesday sales call never reaches the person who has to keep it.
- **It doesn't survive a departure.** When an early salesperson or co-founder leaves, so does every conversation they had.

## Why "add process" usually fails

The instinctive fix is a rule: "Everyone writes up their calls in the CRM." Founders agree to this, mean it, and stop doing it within three weeks. Not because they're careless, but because they have eight meetings a day and writing up each one takes fifteen minutes they don't have.

Any fix that depends on the busiest people in the company doing more admin will fail. The fix has to cost the founder close to zero.

## What works: capture by default, share by default

Teams that solve this tend to land on the same three moves.

**1. Capture is automatic, not optional.** The call gets recorded and transcribed without anyone remembering to do it, through a calendar-connected note taker, the meeting platform's own recording, or (for in-person meetings) a phone or laptop on the table. Always with consent, said out loud at the start.

**2. The output is short and structured.** Nobody reads transcripts. People read a summary with decisions, action items with owners, and the customer's own words on the things that matter (budget, timeline, objections). The Lynkk team wrote about [meeting notes for founders with back-to-back calls](https://lynkk.ai/blog/founders-meeting-notes), including what those notes should hold.

**3. It lives somewhere the team can search.** Not in a founder's inbox. One archive, searchable by customer name or topic. The best version lets anyone ask a question ("what did investors push back on in the last round?") and get an answer that points to the moment it was said. We compared [knowledge management approaches for meeting memory](https://lynkk.ai/blog/meeting-knowledge-management), from wikis to AI search with cited answers.

## What to share and what not to

"Share by default" makes some founders nervous, and fairly so. Not every conversation belongs in a company-wide archive.

A practical split:

- **Share:** customer calls, partner calls, product reviews, team meetings, most investor updates.
- **Keep private:** performance conversations, compensation, early M&A talks, anything a counterpart asked to keep confidential.

Whatever tool you use, make sure a single note can be marked private, and decide the defaults up front rather than call by call.

## The payoff shows up before the next meeting

The most immediate benefit isn't the archive. It's preparation.

When the context from every past call is searchable, preparing for the next one takes two minutes instead of twenty. Before a renewal call, you can pull up what the customer complained about last quarter and what you promised to fix. Before an investor meeting, you can check what they asked last time. Here's a simple [meeting preparation checklist](https://lynkk.ai/blog/meeting-preparation) that builds on exactly this.

And for the first time, someone other than the founder can do that prep.

## A one-week experiment

If you're a founder reading this, try this for one week:

1. Turn on automatic capture for your external calls (with consent).
2. After each call, spend 60 seconds checking the summary, not writing one.
3. Drop every summary in one shared place.
4. At the end of the week, count how many "what did they say about...?" messages you got. Then tell your team to search first.

The goal isn't to stop being in the room. It's to stop being the only place the room is stored.

# Should an AI Bot Be in Your Meeting? An Honest Look at Bots vs Bot-Free Note Takers

*This story was written with AI assistance and edited by the Lynkk team.*

You've seen it. You join a call and there's an extra tile in the grid: "Alex's Notetaker." Nobody says anything about it. Somebody turns their camera off.

AI note takers have become normal fast, and the most visible design choice they make is whether to send a bot into the meeting or record quietly from your own computer. Both approaches have real strengths. Neither is right for every meeting.

## How bot note takers work

A bot note taker joins the call as a participant. It usually connects to your calendar, joins meetings with a Zoom, Google Meet or Teams link when they start, records the audio (sometimes video), and leaves when the call ends. You get a transcript and summary afterwards.

**What bots do well:**

- **They work without your device.** You can send a bot to a call you can't attend.
- **Everyone can see them.** The bot is in the participant list, which is a form of disclosure. Nobody can claim they didn't know a recording tool was present.
- **Speaker names are easy.** Because the bot is inside the meeting, it can often label speakers by their real participant names.
- **They're platform-agnostic.** One bot can join Zoom, Meet and Teams.

**Where bots struggle:**

- **They change the room.** Some people talk less freely with a visible recorder. Some external guests remove the bot, or ask for it to leave.
- **Hosts can block them.** Waiting rooms, lobby settings and admin policies can keep bots out.
- **They don't work in person.** A bot can't join a conference room conversation.

If you're curious about the mechanics, here's how to [add a meeting bot to a Zoom or Google Meet call](https://lynkk.ai/blog/zoom-bot-join-meeting), including what to do when the bot can't get past the waiting room.

## How bot-free note takers work

A bot-free note taker records on your own machine instead. A desktop app or browser extension captures your microphone and the meeting's audio, then transcribes it. There's no extra participant in the call.

**What bot-free capture does well:**

- **No change to the room.** The meeting looks exactly as it did before.
- **Works with any app on your computer**, including ones bots can't join.
- **Works in person.** The same app can record a conversation around a table.

**Where it struggles:**

- **You have to be there.** Your device does the recording.
- **Disclosure is on you.** Because nothing in the call signals that it's being recorded, you must say so yourself. Every time.
- **Speaker labels are harder.** The app knows which voice is yours (your microphone) but has to tell other speakers apart by voice.

## The consent question is the same either way

Here is the part that matters most, and it doesn't depend on the tool.

Recording laws differ by country and by state. Some places require only one person's consent, others require everyone's. A visible bot is not consent. A bot-free recorder is not a loophole. **Say at the start of the call that you're recording, and why.** It takes five seconds and removes almost every awkward moment later.

Any tool marketed as a way to record people "without them noticing" is a tool to avoid.

## Which should you use?

A rough guide:

| Situation | Better fit |
|---|---|
| Internal team meetings you attend | Either; bot-free is lighter |
| Calls you can't attend but need notes from | Bot |
| Sensitive external calls where a visible bot feels heavy | Bot-free, with verbal disclosure |
| Meetings where hosts block bots | Bot-free |
| In-person meetings and interviews | Bot-free |
| Large webinars | Bot, or the platform's own recording |

Many teams end up using both: a bot for routine calls and calls they miss, and a desktop app for everything else. Lynkk, for example, offers a meeting bot for Zoom, Meet and Teams alongside a Mac app and Chrome extension that record without one, and a browser recorder for meetings in the room.

## Platform matters too

Your meeting platform shapes the choice. Zoom has its own AI Companion on paid plans, and Teams has Copilot features for licensed users. These are often the simplest option if you meet on one platform only. They get weaker when you work across several.

If you're on Zoom, there's a comparison of [Zoom note takers](https://lynkk.ai/blog/zoom-note-taker), from AI Companion to bot-free apps. If you're on Teams, here's an overview of [AI note takers for Microsoft Teams](https://lynkk.ai/blog/ai-note-taker-microsoft-teams) and when Copilot is or isn't worth it.

## The short version

Bots are best when you need notes from meetings you can't be in, and when visible disclosure helps. Bot-free is best when you're in the room (virtual or physical) and want the meeting to feel like a meeting. Either way, tell people you're recording. That part isn't a feature; it's manners.

# The Five Minutes Before a Meeting Decide Everything

*This story was written with AI assistance and edited by the Lynkk team.*

Think about the last meeting that went badly. Not catastrophically, just badly. You spent the first ten minutes re-establishing what you'd covered last time. Someone asked about a promise you'd forgotten making. You left without the decision you needed.

Now think about why. Usually it wasn't the agenda. It was that you walked in cold.

## Walking in cold is the default

In a back-to-back day, the gap between meetings is the time it takes to click the next link. There's no room to remember what happened last time with this person or this customer, so you rebuild it live, in front of them.

Most meeting advice focuses on the agenda: send it in advance, keep it short, put decisions first. That's good advice. But an agenda tells you what you're going to talk about. It doesn't tell you what you already know.

## The four questions worth five minutes

Before any meeting that matters (a customer call, a one-on-one, a board prep), it's worth answering four questions. They take about five minutes if your notes are findable and about thirty if they aren't.

**1. What did we decide last time?**
Decisions are the backbone of continuity. If you agreed to a pilot with 15 users, you don't want to re-litigate it.

**2. What did I promise?**
This is the question that saves reputations. "I'll send the security overview by Friday." Did you?

**3. What's still open?**
Unresolved questions from last time are usually the most important items for this time.

**4. What did they say that I might have missed?**
Customers, direct reports and investors say things in passing that turn out to matter: a new stakeholder, a budget change, a frustration. Rereading their exact words often changes your plan.

There's a simple [meeting preparation checklist and brief template](https://lynkk.ai/blog/meeting-preparation) on the Lynkk blog built around these questions.

## Why this is hard without good notes

The four questions are easy to answer if you have a short, structured record of every past meeting with that person or account. They're almost impossible if your record is a mix of half-finished notes, three different recording folders and memory.

That's the real argument for capturing meetings well. Not the archive itself, but the five minutes before the next meeting.

## Where AI assistants actually help

There's a lot of noise about AI meeting assistants. Most of them summarize a meeting after it happens. That's useful, but it's only one of three moments where help matters:

- **Before:** surfacing what was discussed, promised and left open in past meetings with the same people.
- **During:** answering a question in the moment ("what did they say about budget last month?") without leaving the call.
- **After:** summaries, action items with owners, and follow-ups.

A tool that only helps *after* still leaves you walking in cold. When you compare tools, ask what each one does before and during the call, not just after. Our team looked at [8 AI meeting assistants](https://lynkk.ai/blog/ai-powered-meeting-assistants) through exactly that lens. (Our own attempt at the "during" part is Cue, an on-screen helper in the Lynkk Mac app, currently in beta by invite.)

## The one-on-one is the clearest case

Nowhere does preparation matter more than in a one-on-one. Your direct report remembers exactly what they raised last time. If you don't, they notice.

A two-minute review before each one-on-one (what they raised, what you committed to, what's still open) changes the tone of the conversation. It tells them you were listening. If you run regular 1:1s, here are [20 one-on-one meeting questions and a notes template](https://lynkk.ai/blog/one-on-one-meeting) that make this review easy.

## Build the habit in one week

1. **Block five minutes** before your three most important meetings this week. Literally put it in the calendar.
2. **Answer the four questions** for each one, in writing, even if it's three bullet points.
3. **After each meeting**, note one thing the prep changed: a promise you remembered, a topic you raised, a mistake you avoided.

At the end of the week you'll know whether the five minutes earned their place. If they did, keep the block. If they didn't, you've lost fifteen minutes and learned something about your meetings.

# Voice Memos Are the Most Underrated Note-Taking Tool on Your Phone

*This story was written with AI assistance and edited by the Lynkk team.*

Most people open Voice Memos twice a year. It's the app for recording a song idea, a lecture, or a voicemail you want to keep.

That's a waste, because a phone you already carry everywhere, with a decent microphone and a recording app that syncs across devices, is a very good capture tool. Paired with transcription, it becomes a note-taking system that works when typing doesn't: walking, driving (hands-free, please), or sitting across a table from someone.

## Why voice notes beat typed notes in some situations

**You capture more.** Speaking an idea out loud takes seconds. Typing it on a phone keyboard takes long enough that you trim it down, and the trimmed part is often the interesting bit.

**You capture it sooner.** The best time to record a thought is the moment you have it. Voice Memos is one tap from the lock screen with a widget or Control Center button.

**You can capture conversations.** An interview, a site visit, a conversation with a contractor. With permission, a recording is more reliable than your memory of who said what.

## Getting a transcript out of a voice memo

Recent versions of iOS can transcribe Voice Memos recordings directly in the app, on supported devices and languages. You open a recording, tap the transcript option, and the text appears alongside the waveform. You can search and copy it.

When it works, it's great. When it doesn't (the option is missing, the transcript is blank, or your language isn't supported), the cause is usually one of a handful of settings or device limits. The Lynkk team wrote a step-by-step guide to [voice memo transcription on iPhone](https://lynkk.ai/blog/voice-memo-transcription), including how to fix transcription that won't start.

If you need a transcript of an older recording, or one in a language your phone doesn't support, you can export the audio file and run it through a transcription tool. Here's a broader guide to [transcribing any audio to text](https://lynkk.ai/blog/transcribe-audio-to-text), with free options on Mac and Windows and a comparison of paid tools.

## From transcript to notes

A raw transcript isn't a note. It's a pile of words. The trick is a two-minute pass right after recording:

1. **Title it with a who and a what.** "Site visit, Ardmore Foods, warehouse layout" beats "New Recording 47."
2. **Pull out three lines at the top**: the decision, the next step and the open question.
3. **Leave the transcript below** as the source, in case you need the exact words.

If you use a notes app, paste the three lines plus the transcript into one note. In three months, searching "Ardmore" will find it instantly.

## A few habits that make recordings usable

- **Say the context at the start.** "It's Tuesday, I'm with Sam from Ardmore, we're talking about the warehouse layout." Your future self and your transcription tool will both thank you.
- **Put the phone between speakers**, not in your pocket. Distance and fabric are the two biggest enemies of transcript quality.
- **Ask permission when recording other people.** Recording laws vary by place, and asking is simply courteous. Most people say yes when you explain it's so you can listen properly instead of scribbling.
- **Keep recordings short and topical.** Five 5-minute memos are easier to use than one 25-minute ramble.

## When to graduate from Voice Memos

Voice Memos is a great start. It runs out of road when:

- you record **long meetings** every day and want summaries and action items, not just text;
- you need **speaker labels**, so you know who said what;
- you want **one archive** for phone recordings, laptop meetings and online calls;
- you work in **more than one language**, sometimes in the same sentence.

At that point you're choosing between a dedicated recorder device and an app. Devices have a better microphone and a battery that won't die mid-meeting; apps cost less and work with what you already carry. We compared [AI voice recorders, devices vs apps](https://lynkk.ai/blog/ai-voice-recorders), on 12-month cost and transcript quality.

## Try it tomorrow

Next time you leave a meeting, a call or a site visit, open Voice Memos and talk for 60 seconds about what just happened: what was decided, what you need to do and what's still unclear. Transcribe it, title it, and save the three lines.

Do that for a week and you'll have better notes than most people get from an hour of typing.

# How to Choose an AI Note Taker Without Reading 40 Comparison Posts

*This story was written with AI assistance and edited by the Lynkk team. Lynkk makes an AI note taker, so read this with that in mind; the questions below apply whichever tool you pick.*

Search for "best AI note taker" and you'll find dozens of lists. Most rank the same eight or nine tools in a different order, and most are written by one of the companies on the list (including us).

The rankings don't help much, because the right tool depends on how you meet. A sales team on Zoom, a research team doing in-person interviews and a bilingual startup on Google Meet need different things.

So instead of another ranking, here are the six questions that actually decide it. Answer them first and the choice usually narrows to two or three tools.

## 1. Where do your meetings happen?

Start here, because it eliminates the most options.

- **One platform only?** Check what's built in first. Zoom AI Companion, Google Meet's Gemini notes and Copilot in Teams may be enough, if your plan includes them.
- **Several platforms?** You want one tool that covers all of them, or you'll end up with three archives.
- **In person too?** Many tools only work on video calls. If you have conference-room meetings, interviews or site visits, this is a hard filter.

If you're on Zoom today and wondering what else is out there, here's a comparison of [Zoom AI Companion alternatives](https://lynkk.ai/blog/zoom-ai-companion-alternatives), including tools that also cover Meet, Teams and in-person calls.

## 2. Bot or no bot?

Some note takers send a bot into the call as a participant. Others record from your own computer with no bot. Bots work for meetings you can't attend and are visible to everyone. Bot-free tools change nothing about the meeting but require you to be there and to disclose the recording yourself.

Neither is better in general. Decide which your team and your customers are comfortable with.

## 3. What languages do people actually speak?

This question gets skipped and then causes the most frustration. If everyone speaks one language, most tools are fine. If people switch languages mid-sentence, as in Hindi-English (Hinglish) or Spanish-English conversations, many tools produce a mess. Test with a real recording from your own team before you commit.

## 4. Where should the output go?

A summary that sits in the note taker's app is only half useful. Ask:

- Do action items go to your task tracker (Jira, Asana, Linear)?
- Can you get answers in your chat tool (Slack, Teams)?
- Does it update your CRM, or do you copy it there by hand?
- Can you search and ask questions across all past meetings, with links to the source?

Be careful here: "integrates with" can mean anything from a full two-way sync to a button that copies text. Ask what exactly happens.

## 5. What does free actually include?

Free plans vary enormously. Some limit the number of meetings, some limit minutes, some limit how long notes are kept, some limit AI summaries. One tool's "free" covers a light user for months; another's runs out in a week.

Compare the limit that matches how you work. If you have many short meetings, a per-meeting cap hurts. If you have few long ones, a per-minute cap hurts. Our team keeps a comparison of [free AI note taker plans](https://lynkk.ai/blog/best-free-ai-note-takers) that lays out what each one includes and what the upgrade costs.

## 6. What happens to your data?

Ask every vendor, in writing:

- Do you train AI models on our conversations?
- Which third-party providers process our audio and transcripts?
- Where is the data processed, and can we choose?
- Who inside our company can see a note, and is that logged?
- How do we export or delete everything?

If a vendor can't answer clearly, that's an answer.

## Putting it together

Once you've answered the six questions, the field narrows fast. A few examples:

- **Zoom-only sales team, English, wants CRM sync** → shortlist tools with real CRM integrations and test the sync.
- **Product team on Meet and in person, two languages** → in-person capture and code-switching support are must-haves; many popular tools drop out.
- **Solo consultant, few meetings, tight budget** → the best free plan for your meeting pattern matters more than features.

If you're replacing a specific tool, it helps to start from that tool's gaps. For example, here are [Otter.ai alternatives](https://lynkk.ai/blog/otter-ai-alternatives) compared on free limits and fit for sales, product and in-person meetings. And if you do want the full side-by-side, our [AI note taker comparison](https://lynkk.ai/blog/best-ai-note-takers) covers nine tools on free limits, paid plans, bot or bot-free, and platform support.

## Then test, don't read

The last step beats any comparison post: **take two finalists, use each for a week on real meetings, and compare the notes.** Look at how accurate the transcript is, whether the action items are right, and whether anyone on the team actually opened the summary.

That week will tell you more than forty lists.

# How Meeting Bots Actually Join a Zoom, Google Meet or Teams Call

If you've ever had "Someone's Notetaker" appear in your participant list, you've seen a meeting bot. From the outside it looks simple: a fake participant that listens. From the inside, getting a reliable bot into three different platforms is one of the messier problems in applied engineering.

This post walks through the three architectures teams use, the trade-offs of each, and the parts nobody warns you about (waiting rooms, scheduling and consent). It's written from the perspective of building a notetaker, but it applies to anything that needs live meeting audio.

## The three architectures

There are basically three ways to get audio out of a meeting:

1. **Join as a participant through the web client** (a headless browser).
2. **Join through the platform's official bot or media SDK.**
3. **Don't join at all**: pull recordings or transcripts from the platform's API after the meeting.

Most production notetakers use a mix.

## Architecture 1: Headless browser in the web client

Zoom, Google Meet and Teams all have browser clients. A bot can be a real Chromium instance (driven by Playwright or Puppeteer) that navigates to the meeting URL, types a display name, clicks "Join" and then captures the audio that the browser plays.

A minimal join flow looks like this:

```ts
import { chromium } from "playwright";

const browser = await chromium.launch({
  args: [
    "--use-fake-ui-for-media-stream",      // auto-accept mic/camera prompts
    "--use-fake-device-for-media-stream",  // bot has no real devices
    "--autoplay-policy=no-user-gesture-required",
  ],
});
const page = await browser.newPage();
await page.goto(meetingUrl);
await page.getByPlaceholder(/your name/i).fill("Maya's Notetaker");
await page.getByRole("button", { name: /ask to join|join now/i }).click();
```

The selectors above are illustrative. In practice they change whenever the platform ships a UI update, and that's the main cost of this approach.

**Capturing audio.** You have two options:

- **At the OS level**: run the browser on Linux inside a container with a PulseAudio (or PipeWire) null sink as the default output, then record that sink with ffmpeg. Robust and language-agnostic.
- **Inside the page**: inject a script that hooks the `RTCPeerConnection` remote tracks or the `<audio>` elements and pipes them into a `MediaRecorder` or a WebSocket. This gives you per-track audio on some platforms, which helps speaker attribution, but it's fragile.

**Pros:** one codebase pattern for all three platforms; works with any meeting a human could join from a browser.
**Cons:** breaks on UI changes; each bot is a full browser (roughly a CPU core and a few hundred MB of RAM per concurrent meeting); some platforms detect or restrict automated clients.

## Architecture 2: Official SDKs and bot frameworks

Each platform offers a sanctioned path, with very different ergonomics.

**Zoom: Meeting SDK.** The Zoom Meeting SDK (including a Linux build) lets an app join meetings as a participant and, with the right permissions, access raw audio data. Joining meetings outside your own account requires your app to go through Zoom's review. Zoom has also introduced Realtime Media Streams (RTMS), which streams meeting media to an app without a visible participant; check its availability for your account type.

**Microsoft Teams: Graph Communications (calling and meeting bots).** Teams supports bots that join calls and meetings through the Microsoft Graph communications APIs. For raw audio you need *application-hosted media*, which historically means a .NET bot running on Windows Server in Azure, with the Real-time Media Platform. It's powerful and heavy.

**Google Meet: no general-purpose bot SDK.** Meet's official options are the Meet REST API (conference records, recordings and transcripts after the fact) and add-ons that run inside Meet's UI. For live audio, most third-party Meet bots use the browser approach.

**Pros:** supported, more stable than UI automation, sometimes better audio (per-participant streams).
**Cons:** three entirely different stacks; review processes; some require the meeting host's org to approve your app.

## Architecture 3: Skip the bot, use the platform's data

If you don't need live audio, the cheapest bot is no bot. All three platforms can expose recordings or transcripts after the meeting:

- **Zoom** cloud recordings include an audio transcript file (VTT) when that setting is on.
- **Google Meet** transcripts are available through the Meet REST API's `conferenceRecords.transcripts` resources.
- **Teams** transcripts are available through Microsoft Graph's `onlineMeetings/{id}/transcripts`.

This only works when the meeting was recorded or transcribed on a plan that supports it, and only for meetings in tenants that grant you access. It's great for internal tools and useless for meetings hosted by someone else's company.

## The parts nobody warns you about

**Scheduling.** A notetaker that "joins automatically" is really a scheduler reading calendars. You need calendar sync (Google Calendar or Microsoft Graph), a parser that extracts meeting links from event descriptions and conference data, deduplication (three attendees may all have the bot enabled for the same meeting), and a job queue that spins up a worker a minute or so before start time.

**Waiting rooms and lobbies.** Zoom waiting rooms, Meet's "ask to join" and Teams lobbies mean the bot often sits outside until a human admits it. Your bot needs a timeout, a clear display name so the host knows what they're admitting, and a way to tell the user "the bot couldn't get in." We wrote a user-facing guide on [what to do when a Zoom or Meet bot can't join](https://lynkk.ai/blog/zoom-bot-join-meeting) that mirrors these failure modes.

**Leaving.** Bots should leave when the meeting ends, which in practice means "when the bot is the only participant left" or when the platform signals the end. Otherwise you'll record hours of silence.

**Naming and consent.** A bot named after the person who sent it ("Maya's Notetaker") is honest and helps hosts decide whether to admit it. Recording laws vary by jurisdiction, so the product should make it easy for users to tell participants they're recording. Don't build bots designed to go unnoticed.

**Concurrency and cost.** Meetings cluster on the hour. Your infrastructure needs to handle a spike at 9:00, 10:00 and 11:00 local time across every time zone you serve. Autoscale workers ahead of the hour, not reactively.

## How a production notetaker combines these

A typical setup looks like this:

```
Calendar sync ──► Scheduler ──► Bot worker (browser or SDK) ──► Audio chunks
                                                              │
                                     Speech-to-text ◄─────────┘
                                          │
                                 Summary, action items, decisions
                                          │
                              Notes app, email recap, Jira, Slack
```

Lynkk's [meeting bot](https://lynkk.ai/features/meeting-bot), for example, follows Google Calendar and joins Zoom, Meet and Teams calls when they begin, appears under the user's name, and leaves once it's the last one in the call. It doesn't speak or post a consent message, so the product tells users to announce the recording themselves. For users who don't want a bot at all, the same product records from a Mac app or Chrome extension instead, which is a different capture path with its own trade-offs.

## Build or buy?

If you're building a product where meeting audio is an input but not the core, consider a third-party meeting-bot API rather than maintaining three integrations yourself. If live meeting capture *is* your core product, you'll likely end up owning the stack, and you should budget for ongoing maintenance every time a platform ships a UI change.

If your goal is simply notes from your own meetings, you don't need to build anything: built-in tools like Zoom AI Companion, or a third-party notetaker, will do. There's a comparison of [Zoom AI Companion alternatives](https://lynkk.ai/blog/zoom-ai-companion-alternatives) on the Lynkk blog if you want to see how existing products handle bot vs bot-free capture.

## Summary

| Approach | Live audio | Platforms | Main cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| Headless browser | Yes | All three | Breaks on UI changes, heavy per meeting |
| Official SDKs | Yes | One stack each | Three codebases, app reviews |
| Post-meeting APIs | No | All three, with limits | Needs recording/transcripts on, tenant access |

Pick based on whether you need audio *during* the meeting. If you don't, start with the APIs. If you do, expect to maintain it.

# Pulling Google Meet Transcripts With the Meet REST API (Python)

When a Google Meet meeting is transcribed, Meet saves a Google Doc to the organizer's Drive. That's fine for humans, but if you're building anything on top of meetings (search, summaries, a CRM sync) you want structured data: who said what, and when.

The **Google Meet REST API** exposes exactly that. This post shows how to go from a meeting code to a speaker-labelled transcript in Python.

> **Prerequisites.** Transcripts only exist if transcription was turned on during the meeting, on a Google Workspace edition that supports it. If you're not sure whether your plan includes transcripts or where the Doc ends up, start with this non-technical [guide to Google Meet transcripts](https://lynkk.ai/blog/google-meet-transcript).

## The data model in one minute

The API is organized around **conference records**: one record per occurrence of a meeting in a meeting space.

```
spaces/{space}                         the meeting room (has a meeting code)
conferenceRecords/{record}             one occurrence of a meeting
  ├── participants/{participant}       who joined
  ├── recordings/{recording}           video recordings (Drive file)
  └── transcripts/{transcript}         transcript (Google Doc)
        └── entries/{entry}            one utterance: participant, text, start/end time
```

The `entries` collection is what we want. Each entry has a `participant`, the spoken `text`, a `languageCode`, and `startTime`/`endTime`.

## Step 1: Set up a project and OAuth

1. In Google Cloud Console, create a project and **enable the Google Meet REST API**.
2. Configure an OAuth consent screen and create an **OAuth client ID** (Desktop app works for a script).
3. Use a read-only scope: `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/meetings.space.readonly`.

Install dependencies:

```bash
pip install google-auth-oauthlib google-auth requests
```

Get credentials with the installed-app flow:

```python
from google_auth_oauthlib.flow import InstalledAppFlow
from google.auth.transport.requests import Request

SCOPES = ["https://www.googleapis.com/auth/meetings.space.readonly"]

def get_token() -> str:
    flow = InstalledAppFlow.from_client_secrets_file("client_secret.json", SCOPES)
    creds = flow.run_local_server(port=0)
    if not creds.valid:
        creds.refresh(Request())
    return creds.token
```

For production, store and refresh credentials properly rather than running the browser flow every time.

## Step 2: A tiny paginated GET helper

Every list endpoint paginates with `pageToken`, so write one helper:

```python
import requests

BASE = "https://meet.googleapis.com/v2"

def list_all(path: str, token: str, key: str, params: dict | None = None):
    params = dict(params or {})
    headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}"}
    while True:
        r = requests.get(f"{BASE}/{path}", headers=headers, params=params, timeout=30)
        r.raise_for_status()
        data = r.json()
        yield from data.get(key, [])
        token_next = data.get("nextPageToken")
        if not token_next:
            break
        params["pageToken"] = token_next
```

## Step 3: Find the conference record

If you have the meeting code (the `abc-mnop-xyz` part of the Meet link), filter conference records by it:

```python
def conference_records(token: str, meeting_code: str):
    flt = f'space.meeting_code = "{meeting_code}"'
    return list(list_all("conferenceRecords", token, "conferenceRecords", {"filter": flt}))
```

A recurring meeting reuses the same space, so you'll get one record per occurrence. Each has `startTime` and `endTime`; pick the one you want.

## Step 4: Map participants to names

Entries reference participants by resource name, so build a lookup first. Signed-in users have a `signedinUser.displayName`; others may be `anonymousUser` or `phoneUser`.

```python
def participant_names(token: str, record: str) -> dict[str, str]:
    names = {}
    for p in list_all(f"{record}/participants", token, "participants"):
        user = p.get("signedinUser") or p.get("anonymousUser") or p.get("phoneUser") or {}
        names[p["name"]] = user.get("displayName", "Unknown speaker")
    return names
```

## Step 5: Read transcript entries

```python
def transcript_lines(token: str, record: str):
    names = participant_names(token, record)
    for t in list_all(f"{record}/transcripts", token, "transcripts"):
        for e in list_all(f"{t['name']}/entries", token, "transcriptEntries"):
            yield {
                "speaker": names.get(e.get("participant"), "Unknown speaker"),
                "start": e.get("startTime"),
                "text": e.get("text", "").strip(),
            }
```

Note that transcripts move through states (`STARTED`, `ENDED`, `FILE_GENERATED`). Entries can lag behind the end of the meeting, so if you're processing immediately after a call, poll until the transcript has ended.

## Step 6: Write a readable transcript

Merge consecutive entries from the same speaker so the output reads like a conversation:

```python
from datetime import datetime

def to_text(lines) -> str:
    out, last = [], None
    for line in lines:
        ts = datetime.fromisoformat(line["start"].replace("Z", "+00:00")).strftime("%H:%M:%S")
        if line["speaker"] == last:
            out[-1] += " " + line["text"]
        else:
            out.append(f"[{ts}] {line['speaker']}: {line['text']}")
            last = line["speaker"]
    return "\n".join(out)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    tok = get_token()
    rec = conference_records(tok, "abc-mnop-xyz")[-1]["name"]
    print(to_text(transcript_lines(tok, rec)))
```

Output:

```
[14:02:11] Priya Shah: Can we move the rollout to the 28th?
[14:02:16] Dev Patel: Yes, if QA signs off by Friday.
```

## Gotchas

- **No transcript, no data.** If nobody turned transcription on, the `transcripts` list is empty. The API can't transcribe after the fact.
- **Access is scoped to what the user can see.** You'll only get conference records for meetings the authorizing user organized or has access to, within their Workspace.
- **Want it in real time?** The REST API is post-meeting. For notifications when a transcript is ready, look at Google Workspace Events API subscriptions for Meet.
- **Retention follows your Workspace policies.** Don't assume records live forever.

## When this approach isn't enough

The Meet API is ideal for internal tools inside one Workspace. It's a poor fit when:

- you meet across Meet, Zoom and Teams and want one pipeline;
- your plan doesn't include transcripts;
- you need summaries, action items and search, not just text;
- people code-switch between languages, which native captions may not handle well.

That's the gap third-party notetakers fill. If you're evaluating them rather than building, here's a comparison of [AI note takers for Google Meet](https://lynkk.ai/blog/google-meet-ai-note-taker), including Gemini's own notes. Lynkk's [Google Meet integration](https://lynkk.ai/integrations/google-meet) is one example: it records Meet through a bot, a Chrome extension or the Mac app, without needing Workspace transcripts to be turned on.

# Speaker Diarization Explained: Who Said What, With Whisper and pyannote in Python

A transcript without speakers is a wall of text. For a lecture that's fine. For a meeting, an interview or a sales call, it's nearly useless: the whole point is knowing *who* agreed, *who* objected and *who* owns the next step.

**Speaker diarization** answers "who spoke when." It doesn't know names; it splits audio into segments and labels them `SPEAKER_00`, `SPEAKER_01` and so on. Combine it with a speech-to-text model and you get a speaker-labelled transcript.

This post builds that pipeline with two open-source tools, OpenAI's **Whisper** for transcription and **pyannote.audio** for diarization, then covers the real-world problems you'll hit on meeting audio.

## How diarization works (briefly)

Modern diarization pipelines do roughly four things:

1. **Voice activity detection**: find where anyone is speaking.
2. **Segmentation**: split speech into short chunks, detecting speaker changes and overlaps.
3. **Embedding**: turn each chunk into a vector that represents the voice (a "speaker embedding").
4. **Clustering**: group chunks whose embeddings are similar, so each cluster is one speaker.

The output is a timeline: `0.5s to 4.2s SPEAKER_00`, `4.3s to 9.8s SPEAKER_01`, and so on.

Transcription models like Whisper produce a different timeline: text segments with start and end times. Our job is to align the two.

## Setup

```bash
pip install openai-whisper pyannote.audio
# ffmpeg is required by Whisper
brew install ffmpeg   # or apt-get install ffmpeg
```

pyannote's pretrained pipelines are gated on Hugging Face: accept the model's terms on its model page and create an access token.

Convert your input to 16 kHz mono WAV first; both tools are happier with it:

```bash
ffmpeg -i meeting.m4a -ac 1 -ar 16000 meeting.wav
```

## Step 1: Transcribe with Whisper

```python
import whisper

asr = whisper.load_model("small")          # try "medium" or "large" for accuracy
result = asr.transcribe("meeting.wav")
segments = result["segments"]              # each has start, end, text
```

## Step 2: Diarize with pyannote

```python
import os
from pyannote.audio import Pipeline

pipeline = Pipeline.from_pretrained(
    "pyannote/speaker-diarization-3.1",
    use_auth_token=os.environ["HF_TOKEN"],  # newer releases name this `token`
)
diarization = pipeline("meeting.wav")       # optionally num_speakers=3

turns = [
    (turn.start, turn.end, speaker)
    for turn, _, speaker in diarization.itertracks(yield_label=True)
]
```

If you know how many people were in the meeting, pass `num_speakers` (or `min_speakers`/`max_speakers`). It's the single cheapest accuracy win.

## Step 3: Assign a speaker to each transcript segment

The simplest robust approach: for each Whisper segment, pick the speaker whose turns overlap it the most.

```python
from collections import defaultdict

def overlap(a0, a1, b0, b1):
    return max(0.0, min(a1, b1) - max(a0, b0))

def label_segments(segments, turns):
    labelled = []
    for seg in segments:
        scores = defaultdict(float)
        for t0, t1, spk in turns:
            scores[spk] += overlap(seg["start"], seg["end"], t0, t1)
        speaker = max(scores, key=scores.get) if scores else "UNKNOWN"
        labelled.append({**seg, "speaker": speaker})
    return labelled

def merge_turns(labelled):
    merged = []
    for seg in labelled:
        if merged and merged[-1]["speaker"] == seg["speaker"]:
            merged[-1]["text"] += seg["text"]
            merged[-1]["end"] = seg["end"]
        else:
            merged.append(dict(seg))
    return merged

for s in merge_turns(label_segments(segments, turns)):
    print(f"[{s['start']:7.1f}] {s['speaker']}: {s['text'].strip()}")
```

Output looks like:

```
[    2.1] SPEAKER_00: Can we move the rollout to the 28th?
[    6.4] SPEAKER_01: Yes, if QA signs off by Friday.
```

Segment-level assignment is coarse: a single Whisper segment can contain two speakers. For finer results, use word-level timestamps (`word_timestamps=True` in Whisper) and assign speakers per word, or use a toolkit like WhisperX that does alignment for you.

## Why meeting audio is harder than benchmarks

Diarization looks great on clean podcast audio and gets noticeably worse in real meetings. The usual culprits:

- **Overlapping speech.** People interrupt, agree ("mm-hm") and talk over each other. Overlaps are where diarization errors cluster.
- **Short turns.** "Yes." "Agreed." Half-second turns don't give the embedding model much to work with.
- **Similar voices.** Two speakers of similar age and accent on similar microphones can merge into one cluster.
- **Room audio.** In-person meetings recorded from one laptop add echo and distance, and quieter speakers get lost.
- **Compression.** Conferencing codecs are tuned for intelligibility, not for preserving voice characteristics.

## Practical tricks that help a lot

**Use separate channels when you can.** If you record the local microphone and the remote call audio on separate channels, you already know which speech is "you" with no diarization at all, and you only need to diarize the remote side. Many desktop notetakers record exactly this way for that reason.

**Use participant metadata.** Meeting platforms know who is unmuted and who has the active-speaker indicator. A bot inside the call can use that to map clusters to real names. That's why bot-based notetakers can often show real participant names.

**Constrain the number of speakers.** Calendar invites tell you who's expected. Use it.

**Map clusters to names after the fact.** Let users rename `SPEAKER_01` to "Priya" once, then propagate that label across the transcript.

## Diarization in interviews and research

Speaker labels matter most in one-to-one and small-group recordings: user interviews, hiring interviews, customer discovery. In a UX interview you need to separate the participant's words from the interviewer's prompts, or your analysis will quote your own leading questions back at you. Lynkk has a write-up on transcribing [user interviews for research](https://lynkk.ai/use-cases/user-interviews) that covers this from the researcher's side.

## Build vs use

This pipeline is a good way to understand the problem, and it's fine for batch processing a folder of recordings. For production you'll also need chunking for long files, GPU scheduling, language detection, and a UI for corrections.

If you just need transcripts, the Lynkk team compared [7 AI transcription tools](https://lynkk.ai/blog/ai-transcription-software) by job (live transcripts, file uploads, editing by text, meeting notes), and there's a more general guide on [how to transcribe audio to text](https://lynkk.ai/blog/transcribe-audio-to-text) with free options.

## Summary

- Transcription answers *what*, diarization answers *who*.
- Align them by time overlap; go word-level for accuracy.
- Meeting audio is hard because of overlaps, short turns and room acoustics.
- Separate channels and platform metadata beat clever clustering.

# Code-Switching Breaks Speech Recognition: How to Test Hinglish ASR With WER and CER

Listen to a product meeting in Bengaluru, a sales call in Mumbai or a standup at almost any Indian startup and you'll hear sentences like this:

> "Kal ka deployment thoda delay ho gaya, but QA ne sign off de diya hai, so we can push it today."

That's **Hinglish**: Hindi and English mixed inside the same sentence. Linguists call it *code-switching*. Speech recognition systems, especially ones that ask you to pick one language per recording, often handle it badly.

If you're choosing or building an ASR system for this kind of audio, you need to measure it properly. This post builds a small evaluation harness and explains the trap that makes most Hinglish benchmarks meaningless.

## Why code-switching is hard for ASR

- **Language identification fights you.** Many systems detect one language per file or per segment, then decode everything as that language. English words in a Hindi-detected segment get forced into Hindi spellings, and vice versa.
- **Vocabulary is mixed.** Technical and business terms ("deployment", "sign off", "pipeline") arrive in English inside Hindi grammar.
- **Training data is scarce.** Clean Hindi and clean English audio are abundant. Natural code-switched conversational audio with good transcripts is much rarer.
- **There's no single correct spelling.** Which brings us to the real problem.

## The script problem

The same spoken Hinglish sentence can be written at least three valid ways:

1. **All Devanagari:** "कल का डिप्लॉयमेंट थोड़ा डिले हो गया"
2. **All Roman (Latin script):** "kal ka deployment thoda delay ho gaya"
3. **Mixed script:** "कल का deployment थोड़ा delay हो गया"

If your reference transcript is in one style and the model outputs another, **word error rate will look catastrophic even when the transcription is perfect.** Every word counts as a substitution.

So the first rule of Hinglish evaluation: **decide the target script convention before you write a single reference transcript, and normalize both sides to it.** For meeting notes read by people who type in Roman script on their phones, Roman or mixed script is usually what users want. For formal Hindi documents, Devanagari may be right. There's no universal answer, but there must be *an* answer.

## Building the harness

```bash
pip install jiwer
```

### 1. A test set that looks like your users

Record or collect 20 to 50 short clips (30 to 90 seconds) of real conversational audio: meetings, calls, interviews, with consent. Include:

- pure Hindi, pure English and heavily mixed clips;
- a range of accents and speaking speeds;
- laptop microphones, phone audio and conference-room audio.

Have a fluent bilingual person transcribe each clip **in your chosen script convention**. Store them as pairs:

```
data/
  clip_001.wav
  clip_001.ref.txt
  ...
```

### 2. Normalization

WER is extremely sensitive to casing, punctuation and spacing. Normalize consistently:

```python
import re
import unicodedata

def normalize(text: str) -> str:
    text = unicodedata.normalize("NFC", text)
    text = text.lower()
    text = re.sub(r"[^\w\sऀ-ॿ]", " ", text)   # keep word chars and Devanagari
    text = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", text).strip()
    return text
```

If your convention is Roman script but some system outputs Devanagari, you'll need a transliteration step before scoring. Be explicit about whether you're scoring the system's raw output or its output after transliteration. They answer different questions.

### 3. Score WER and CER

```python
from pathlib import Path
import jiwer

def score(refs: list[str], hyps: list[str]) -> dict:
    refs = [normalize(r) for r in refs]
    hyps = [normalize(h) for h in hyps]
    return {
        "wer": jiwer.wer(refs, hyps),
        "cer": jiwer.cer(refs, hyps),
    }

def load_pairs(data_dir: str, hyp_suffix: str):
    refs, hyps = [], []
    for ref_path in sorted(Path(data_dir).glob("*.ref.txt")):
        hyp_path = ref_path.with_name(ref_path.name.replace(".ref.txt", hyp_suffix))
        refs.append(ref_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
        hyps.append(hyp_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    return refs, hyps

refs, hyps = load_pairs("data", ".system_a.txt")
print(score(refs, hyps))
```

**Report CER alongside WER.** Character error rate is more forgiving of small spelling variation ("thoda" vs "thora"), which is common in romanized Hindi. If WER is high but CER is low, the system is probably right but spelling things differently from your references.

### 4. Break results down by switch density

An average hides the problem you care about. Tag each clip with a rough code-switch ratio (the share of words in the minority language) and report per bucket:

```python
def english_ratio(ref: str, english_vocab: set[str]) -> float:
    words = normalize(ref).split()
    return sum(w in english_vocab for w in words) / max(len(words), 1)
```

A crude English wordlist is enough for bucketing. You'll often find a system that scores well on pure Hindi and pure English and falls apart in the 20 to 50% mixed bucket, which is exactly where real meetings live.

## What to look for beyond WER

Error rates aren't the whole story for meeting notes. Also check:

- **Named entities**: people, companies, product names. A single wrong client name is worse than five wrong filler words.
- **Numbers and dates**: "28 tareekh" vs "the 28th". Downstream action items depend on these.
- **English technical terms inside Hindi sentences**: are they preserved, or transliterated into nonsense?
- **Summary quality**: if the transcript feeds an LLM summary, evaluate the summary too. Sometimes a summarizer recovers from transcript errors; sometimes it confidently invents things.

## A note on choosing a tool

If you're evaluating products rather than models, ask vendors three questions:

1. Do you support code-switched audio in one recording, or do I pick one language?
2. What script does the transcript come out in, and can I choose?
3. Can I test with my own audio before committing?

Lynkk, for example, offers a dedicated [Hinglish transcription mode](https://lynkk.ai/features/hinglish-transcription) for people who switch between Hindi and English mid-sentence, alongside [17 languages](https://lynkk.ai/features/multilingual-transcription) with auto-detect. Whatever you evaluate, run it on your own clips with the harness above. For non-technical readers looking for free options, the Lynkk blog has a guide to [Hindi transcription in India](https://lynkk.ai/blog/hindi-transcription), including Google Docs, YouTube and Hinglish meetings.

## Summary

- Code-switching breaks the one-language-per-file assumption.
- Fix the script convention first, or your WER is meaningless.
- Report WER and CER, and break results down by switch density.
- Check names, numbers and technical terms, not just averages.
