# From Meeting Action Items to Jira Issues: A Small Python Service

Every engineering team has the same leak: a decision gets made in a meeting, someone says "I'll take that," and the task never makes it into Jira. Two sprints later nobody remembers who owned it.

This post builds a small service that takes structured action items from meeting notes and creates Jira issues with an assignee, due date, priority and enough context to be useful. It's deliberately provider-agnostic: the action items can come from a human-written summary, an AI notetaker's export, or an LLM you run yourself.

## The shape of a good action item

Before writing code, agree on what an action item is. A useful one has:

- **one owner** (not "the team");
- **a verb-first summary** ("Send revised pricing draft to Sam");
- **a due date** if one was stated;
- **a priority** if one was implied;
- **a link back to the moment in the meeting** where it was agreed.

If your notes don't capture those, no amount of automation helps. There's a good list of [action item examples and a template](https://lynkk.ai/blog/action-items-examples-template) for calibrating what "good" looks like.

We'll use this schema:

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Optional

@dataclass
class ActionItem:
    summary: str                  # "Send revised pricing draft to Sam"
    owner_email: Optional[str]    # "dana@acme.com"
    due_date: Optional[str]       # "2026-10-29" (ISO)
    priority: Optional[str]       # "High" | "Medium" | "Low"
    meeting_title: str            # "Acme pilot kickoff"
    meeting_url: str              # link to the note or recording
    quote: str                    # the sentence where it was agreed
    timestamp: str                # "00:24:10"
```

## Step 1: Get structured action items

**Option A: from a notetaker.** Many notetakers export notes as Markdown or JSON with action items, owners and timestamps. Map their fields to `ActionItem`.

**Option B: from a transcript with an LLM.** If you're extracting yourself, ask for strict JSON and validate it. A prompt that works well across models:

```text
From the meeting transcript below, list every action item that someone
explicitly agreed to do. Return JSON only, as a list of objects with keys:
summary (imperative, under 12 words), owner_name, due_date (ISO date or null),
priority (High/Medium/Low or null), quote (the exact sentence), timestamp.
Do not invent owners or dates. If no owner was stated, use null.
```

Two rules matter more than prompt wording: **validate the JSON against your schema**, and **never invent owners**. An unassigned issue is better than one assigned to the wrong person.

## Step 2: Resolve owners to Jira account IDs

Jira Cloud assigns issues by `accountId`, not email. Look people up with the user search endpoint:

```python
import os
import requests

JIRA = os.environ["JIRA_BASE_URL"]          # https://your-domain.atlassian.net
AUTH = (os.environ["JIRA_EMAIL"], os.environ["JIRA_API_TOKEN"])
HEADERS = {"Accept": "application/json", "Content-Type": "application/json"}

_cache: dict[str, str | None] = {}

def account_id_for(email: str | None) -> str | None:
    if not email:
        return None
    if email in _cache:
        return _cache[email]
    r = requests.get(f"{JIRA}/rest/api/3/user/search",
                     params={"query": email}, auth=AUTH, headers=HEADERS, timeout=20)
    r.raise_for_status()
    users = r.json()
    _cache[email] = users[0]["accountId"] if users else None
    return _cache[email]
```

Email visibility depends on each user's Atlassian privacy settings, so lookups can return nothing. Fall back to leaving the issue unassigned and mentioning the owner's name in the description.

## Step 3: Write a description in Atlassian Document Format

Jira Cloud's v3 API expects descriptions in ADF (a JSON document format), not Markdown. Keep it simple: context, the quote, and a link.

```python
def adf_description(item: ActionItem) -> dict:
    def para(*nodes):
        return {"type": "paragraph", "content": list(nodes)}
    def text(t, marks=None):
        node = {"type": "text", "text": t}
        if marks:
            node["marks"] = marks
        return node

    return {
        "type": "doc",
        "version": 1,
        "content": [
            para(text("From meeting: "), text(item.meeting_title, [{"type": "strong"}])),
            para(text(f"Agreed at {item.timestamp}: "), text(f"“{item.quote}”", [{"type": "em"}])),
            para(text("Source note", [{"type": "link", "attrs": {"href": item.meeting_url}}])),
        ],
    }
```

The quote and the link are what make the issue useful to someone who wasn't there. Without them, "Send revised pricing draft" a week later is a mystery.

## Step 4: Create the issue

```python
def create_issue(item: ActionItem, project_key: str, issue_type: str = "Task") -> str:
    fields = {
        "project": {"key": project_key},
        "issuetype": {"name": issue_type},
        "summary": item.summary,
        "description": adf_description(item),
        "labels": ["from-meeting"],
    }
    if item.due_date:
        fields["duedate"] = item.due_date
    if item.priority:
        fields["priority"] = {"name": item.priority}
    if (acct := account_id_for(item.owner_email)):
        fields["assignee"] = {"id": acct}

    r = requests.post(f"{JIRA}/rest/api/3/issue",
                      json={"fields": fields}, auth=AUTH, headers=HEADERS, timeout=20)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()["key"]
```

Field availability depends on the project's screen configuration. If `duedate` or `priority` aren't on the create screen, Jira rejects the request; check with `GET /rest/api/3/issue/createmeta` or simply add them to the screen.

## Step 5: Make it idempotent

Meetings get re-processed. Notes get edited. You don't want duplicate issues. Store a stable key per action item (for example a hash of meeting ID + timestamp + summary) and skip items you've already created:

```python
import hashlib, json, pathlib

STATE = pathlib.Path("created.json")
seen = json.loads(STATE.read_text()) if STATE.exists() else {}

def item_key(item: ActionItem) -> str:
    raw = f"{item.meeting_url}|{item.timestamp}|{item.summary.lower()}"
    return hashlib.sha256(raw.encode()).hexdigest()[:16]

def sync(items: list[ActionItem], project_key: str):
    for item in items:
        k = item_key(item)
        if k in seen:
            continue
        seen[k] = create_issue(item, project_key)
        print("created", seen[k], item.summary)
    STATE.write_text(json.dumps(seen, indent=2))
```

## Step 6: Keep a human in the loop

Fully automatic issue creation sounds great and produces noise. Meetings generate "action items" that were jokes, hypotheticals or things already done. A better default: **create issues only after someone presses a button** on the meeting summary, or post the proposed issues to a Slack thread for a thumbs-up first.

That's also how most notetakers that integrate with Jira work. Lynkk's [Jira integration](https://lynkk.ai/integrations/jira), for instance, creates one issue per action item, in the project and issue type you choose, when you press Send on a note.

## Where this fits in the bigger picture

Getting action items into Jira is the last mile. The earlier miles are capturing the meeting and writing minutes that hold decisions as well as tasks. For the non-code side, including whether minutes need to be verbatim, see [how product teams turn meeting minutes into Jira issues](https://lynkk.ai/blog/meeting-minutes-to-jira).

# Capturing System Audio on macOS Without a Virtual Driver: Core Audio Taps (macOS 14.2+)

For years, recording "what the Mac is playing" meant installing a virtual audio driver, rerouting your output through it and hoping users understood the setup. That's why so many meeting tools chose to send a bot into the call instead.

Since **macOS 14.2**, Apple ships a first-party API for this: **Core Audio process taps**. An app can tap the audio output of specific processes (or everything except some processes) and read it like an input device, with a system permission prompt instead of a kernel extension.

This post explains the three generations of approaches, then sketches the tap-based one in Swift.

> The code below is a sketch with error handling removed for readability. Apple's sample code for Core Audio taps is the authoritative reference. And as always with recording: tell the people on the call.

## Three generations of "record the Mac's audio"

**1. Virtual audio drivers (any macOS).** Tools like BlackHole or Loopback install an audio device. Users route output to it (often through a multi-output device so they can still hear). It works, but setup is fragile and confusing, and it needs a driver install.

**2. ScreenCaptureKit audio (macOS 13+).** `SCStream` can capture app or display audio alongside screen content by setting `capturesAudio = true` on the stream configuration. No driver needed, but it requires the **Screen Recording** permission, which is a big ask for an app that only wants audio and makes users understandably nervous.

**3. Core Audio process taps (macOS 14.2+).** Purpose-built for audio. The permission is "System Audio Recording Only", which is a much easier conversation with users, and you can target specific processes.

That third option is why a number of Mac meeting recorders list **macOS 14.2 or later** as a requirement.

## How a process tap works

The flow has four pieces:

1. **Describe the tap** with `CATapDescription`: which processes to include or exclude, mono or stereo, and whether to mute the original output.
2. **Create the tap** with `AudioHardwareCreateProcessTap`, which returns an `AudioObjectID`.
3. **Wrap it in a private aggregate device** whose tap list contains your tap's UUID.
4. **Read buffers** from the aggregate device with an IO proc, like any input device.

## Step 1: Find the process you want

Taps target Core Audio *process objects*, not PIDs. Translate a PID with `kAudioHardwarePropertyTranslatePIDToProcessObject`:

```swift
import CoreAudio

func audioProcessObject(for pid: pid_t) -> AudioObjectID? {
    var address = AudioObjectPropertyAddress(
        mSelector: kAudioHardwarePropertyTranslatePIDToProcessObject,
        mScope: kAudioObjectPropertyScopeGlobal,
        mElement: kAudioObjectPropertyElementMain)
    var pid = pid
    var objectID = AudioObjectID(kAudioObjectUnknown)
    var size = UInt32(MemoryLayout<AudioObjectID>.size)
    let status = AudioObjectGetPropertyData(
        AudioObjectID(kAudioObjectSystemObject), &address,
        UInt32(MemoryLayout<pid_t>.size), &pid, &size, &objectID)
    return status == noErr && objectID != kAudioObjectUnknown ? objectID : nil
}
```

Get the PID from `NSRunningApplication` for the meeting app (for example by bundle identifier). For a browser-based meeting you'd tap the browser process.

## Step 2: Create the tap

```swift
let processes = [zoomProcessObject]            // [AudioObjectID]
let description = CATapDescription(stereoMixdownOfProcesses: processes)
description.uuid = UUID()
description.isPrivate = true
description.muteBehavior = .unmuted            // user keeps hearing the call

var tapID = AudioObjectID(kAudioObjectUnknown)
let err = AudioHardwareCreateProcessTap(description, &tapID)
```

Alternatively, `CATapDescription(stereoGlobalTapButExcludeProcesses: [ownProcess])` taps everything except your own app, which avoids recording your app's sounds.

## Step 3: Put the tap in a private aggregate device

```swift
let aggregateUID = UUID().uuidString
let config: [String: Any] = [
    kAudioAggregateDeviceNameKey: "Meeting Tap",
    kAudioAggregateDeviceUIDKey: aggregateUID,
    kAudioAggregateDeviceIsPrivateKey: true,
    kAudioAggregateDeviceTapAutoStartKey: true,
    kAudioAggregateDeviceTapListKey: [
        [kAudioSubTapUIDKey: description.uuid.uuidString]
    ],
]

var aggregateID = AudioObjectID(kAudioObjectUnknown)
AudioHardwareCreateAggregateDevice(config as CFDictionary, &aggregateID)
```

A private aggregate device doesn't appear in the user's Sound settings, which is what you want.

## Step 4: Read audio

```swift
var procID: AudioDeviceIOProcID?
let queue = DispatchQueue(label: "tap.io")

AudioDeviceCreateIOProcIDWithBlock(&procID, aggregateID, queue) { _, inInputData, _, _, _ in
    // inInputData is an UnsafePointer<AudioBufferList> of float samples.
    // Copy it out quickly: append to a ring buffer, an AVAudioFile, or an encoder.
    writer.append(inInputData)
}
AudioDeviceStart(aggregateID, procID)
```

Read the tap's format (`kAudioTapPropertyFormat`) so you know the sample rate and channel layout before writing files. When you're done, stop the device, destroy the IO proc, the aggregate device and the tap, in that order.

## Permission and Info.plist

Add `NSAudioCaptureUsageDescription` to your Info.plist with a clear, honest sentence ("Lets the app record the audio of calls you choose to record, so it can write your meeting notes"). The first tap creation triggers the system prompt. If the user declines, creation fails and you should explain how to re-enable it in System Settings, Privacy and Security.

## Add the microphone as a second channel

The tap gives you the *remote* side of the call. Capture the user's microphone separately (with `AVAudioEngine`'s input node or an `AVCaptureSession`) and store it on its own channel or track. As with browser recorders, two channels mean you always know which speech is the user's, and you only diarize the remote side.

## Detecting calls

Most bot-free recorders don't record all the time. They watch for a meeting app starting a call (often by watching for an app to begin using the microphone, together with knowing which apps are meeting apps) and then *ask* the user: record, or not now. Asking is better UX and better ethics than auto-recording everything.

## Production notes

- **Sample-rate mismatches**: the tap's rate may differ from the mic's. Resample before mixing.
- **Device changes**: AirPods connecting mid-call changes the output device. Listen for property changes and rebuild if needed.
- **Offline resilience**: write to disk continuously so a dropped network connection or crash doesn't lose the recording; upload later.
- **Apple silicon and OS version**: gate the feature on macOS 14.2+ and fail gracefully below that.

## Where you'll see this in practice

Lynkk's [Mac app](https://lynkk.ai/download) is one example of a bot-free recorder: it notices calls in Zoom, Teams, Webex, FaceTime, Slack huddles and WhatsApp, plus Meet, Zoom, Teams and Webex in the browser, asks whether to record (or records automatically, if the user chooses), and keeps the microphone and the call audio on separate channels. It requires Apple silicon and macOS 14.2 or later. The same app does [dictation](https://lynkk.ai/features/dictation) in any text field, which is a different audio path: microphone in, text out. If you just want to use built-in dictation, here's a guide to [dictation on Mac](https://lynkk.ai/blog/dictation-on-mac) and how to fix it when it stops working.

# Ask Your Meetings: Building Q&A Over Transcripts With Timestamped Citations

"What did the customer say about their security review?" is a simple question with an annoying answer: it's somewhere in one of forty calls. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over meeting transcripts can answer it, but only if users can **check** the answer. In meetings, a confident wrong answer ("they approved the budget") is worse than no answer.

This post builds a small Q&A pipeline over transcripts where every claim carries a citation to a specific meeting and timestamp, and the code verifies those citations before showing anything. It's provider-agnostic: plug in whichever embedding model and LLM you use.

## Why meetings are different from documents

Most RAG tutorials chunk documents by token count. Meeting transcripts have structure you should keep:

- **Speakers matter.** "We can stretch to $50K" means something different from the customer than from your own rep.
- **Time matters.** Users want to jump to the moment and hear it.
- **Decisions change.** The budget was $30K in discovery and $50K three weeks later. The latest statement usually wins, but both are useful.
- **Transcripts are noisy.** Filler words, crosstalk and recognition errors are normal.

So we'll chunk by **speaker turns**, keep **meeting metadata and timestamps** on every chunk, and include **dates** in the prompt.

## Step 1: Chunk by speaker turn

Assume each transcript is a list of utterances `{speaker, start, text}` (any notetaker export or your own diarized output works).

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Chunk:
    id: str
    meeting_id: str
    meeting_title: str
    meeting_date: str      # ISO date
    start: str             # "00:18:42"
    speakers: list[str]
    text: str

def chunk_meeting(meeting, max_chars=900, overlap_turns=1):
    turns = meeting["utterances"]
    chunks, buf = [], []
    def flush():
        if not buf:
            return
        chunks.append(Chunk(
            id=f"{meeting['id']}:{len(chunks)}",
            meeting_id=meeting["id"],
            meeting_title=meeting["title"],
            meeting_date=meeting["date"],
            start=buf[0]["start"],
            speakers=sorted({t["speaker"] for t in buf}),
            text="\n".join(f"{t['speaker']}: {t['text']}" for t in buf),
        ))
    for t in turns:
        buf.append(t)
        if sum(len(x["text"]) for x in buf) > max_chars:
            flush()
            buf = buf[-overlap_turns:]   # keep context across chunk boundaries
    flush()
    return chunks
```

Overlapping by one turn keeps question-and-answer pairs together ("What's your budget?" / "Around $30K.") more often than not.

## Step 2: Embed and index

Any sentence-embedding model works. Here's the pattern with `sentence-transformers` and plain NumPy:

```python
import numpy as np
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")

def build_index(chunks):
    texts = [f"{c.meeting_title} ({c.meeting_date})\n{c.text}" for c in chunks]
    vecs = model.encode(texts, normalize_embeddings=True)
    return np.asarray(vecs), chunks

def search(index, query, k=8):
    vecs, chunks = index
    q = model.encode([query], normalize_embeddings=True)[0]
    scores = vecs @ q
    top = np.argsort(-scores)[:k]
    return [(chunks[i], float(scores[i])) for i in top]
```

For real use, add **hybrid search** (BM25 plus embeddings). Customer names, product codes and numbers are exactly where pure embedding search is weakest, and they're exactly what people ask about.

## Step 3: Prompt for cited answers

Number the retrieved chunks and require the model to cite them inline:

```python
def build_prompt(question, hits):
    sources = []
    for n, (c, _) in enumerate(hits, 1):
        sources.append(
            f"[{n}] {c.meeting_title}, {c.meeting_date}, at {c.start}\n{c.text}"
        )
    return f"""Answer the question using only the sources below.
After every sentence that states a fact, add the source number in brackets, like [2].
If sources disagree, prefer the most recent and say that it changed.
If the sources do not contain the answer, say you could not find it.

Sources:
{chr(10).join(sources)}

Question: {question}
Answer:"""
```

Then call your LLM of choice:

```python
answer = call_llm(build_prompt(question, hits))   # provider-agnostic
```

## Step 4: Verify citations before showing them

Never trust the model's citation markers blindly. At minimum:

```python
import re

def verify(answer: str, hits) -> tuple[bool, list[int]]:
    if "could not find" in answer.lower():
        return True, []
    cited = sorted({int(n) for n in re.findall(r"\[(\d+)\]", answer)})
    valid = [n for n in cited if 1 <= n <= len(hits)]
    # Every marker must point at a real source, and there must be at least one.
    return bool(cited) and len(valid) == len(cited), valid
```

If verification fails, retry once with a stricter instruction, or fall back to showing the top retrieved snippets without a generated answer. A list of relevant quotes is a perfectly good answer when synthesis isn't trustworthy.

For stronger checks, verify that each cited chunk actually *supports* the sentence, for example with a second, cheap model call that answers yes or no per sentence-source pair.

## Step 5: Render citations as links to moments

Each citation becomes a link to the meeting at a timestamp, so the user can hear it:

```python
def render(answer, hits, base="https://notes.example.com"):
    def link(m):
        n = int(m.group(1))
        c = hits[n - 1][0]
        return f"[[{n}]]({base}/{c.meeting_id}?t={c.start})"
    return re.sub(r"\[(\d+)\]", link, answer)
```

This is the part users care about most. A cited answer they can verify in five seconds builds trust; an uncited answer, however fluent, gets ignored after the first mistake.

## Permissions are part of retrieval

In a team setting, retrieval must respect who can see which meeting. Filter chunks by the asker's access **before** search, not after generation. Otherwise a model can paraphrase content from a meeting the user isn't allowed to see. Private notes, HR conversations and confidential calls must never enter the candidate set for someone without access.

## What good looks like

A production version of this is what some notetakers now ship as a feature. Lynkk's [Ask Lynkk](https://lynkk.ai/features/ask-your-meetings) (a Pro feature), for instance, answers questions across your notes with numbered sources you can open down to the moment in the recording, reads only the asker's own notes (plus, for workspace admins, notes members left visible to admins), and only drafts a Jira issue or calendar event after the user confirms. Sales teams use the same idea for deal reviews and call prep; there's more on that in this overview of [conversation intelligence for sales teams](https://lynkk.ai/blog/sales-conversation-intelligence).

For the broader, non-technical picture of turning meetings into team memory (wikis, search, cited answers), see [knowledge management tools for meeting memory](https://lynkk.ai/blog/meeting-knowledge-management).

## Summary

- Chunk by speaker turn and keep meeting, date and timestamp metadata.
- Use hybrid search; names and numbers matter most.
- Force inline citations, then verify them in code.
- Link each citation to the exact moment.
- Enforce access control before retrieval.

---

# Getting Microsoft Teams Meeting Transcripts With the Graph API

When transcription is turned on in a Teams meeting, Microsoft stores the transcript and exposes it through **Microsoft Graph**. If you're building internal tooling (a summary bot, a searchable archive, a CRM sync), you can fetch those transcripts programmatically instead of asking people to download files.

This post covers the permissions, the endpoints, the WebVTT format Teams uses, and change notifications so you don't have to poll.

> Transcripts only exist if someone turned on transcription (or recording with transcription) in the meeting, and your tenant's policies allow it. Graph can't transcribe audio after the fact.

## Permissions

Transcript access uses the `OnlineMeetingTranscript.Read.All` permission.

- **Delegated** (acting as a signed-in user): the user can read transcripts of meetings they organized or attended, subject to policy.
- **Application** (a daemon with no user): needs admin consent **and** an **application access policy** that a Teams admin assigns, allowing your app to read meetings on behalf of specific users. Without the policy, calls fail even with the permission granted.

You'll typically also need `OnlineMeetings.Read` (or `.All`) to look meetings up.

## Step 1: Resolve the meeting from its join URL

Graph identifies meetings by an `onlineMeeting` ID, not the URL people paste. Look it up by `JoinWebUrl`:

```python
import requests

GRAPH = "https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0"

def meeting_id_from_join_url(token: str, user_id: str, join_url: str) -> str:
    r = requests.get(
        f"{GRAPH}/users/{user_id}/onlineMeetings",
        headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}"},
        params={"$filter": f"JoinWebUrl eq '{join_url}'"},
        timeout=30,
    )
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()["value"][0]["id"]
```

With delegated auth you can use `/me/onlineMeetings` instead of `/users/{id}/onlineMeetings`. Get the token with MSAL (`msal` package) using whichever flow matches your app.

## Step 2: List and download transcripts

A meeting can have several transcripts (for example if transcription was stopped and restarted).

```python
def list_transcripts(token, user_id, meeting_id):
    r = requests.get(
        f"{GRAPH}/users/{user_id}/onlineMeetings/{meeting_id}/transcripts",
        headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}"}, timeout=30)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()["value"]

def transcript_vtt(token, user_id, meeting_id, transcript_id) -> str:
    r = requests.get(
        f"{GRAPH}/users/{user_id}/onlineMeetings/{meeting_id}"
        f"/transcripts/{transcript_id}/content",
        headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}"},
        params={"$format": "text/vtt"}, timeout=60)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.text
```

## Step 3: Parse Teams' WebVTT

Teams transcripts use WebVTT with **voice tags** for speakers:

```
WEBVTT

00:00:02.120 --> 00:00:05.480
<v Priya Shah>Can we move the rollout to the 28th?</v>

00:00:06.010 --> 00:00:08.300
<v Dev Patel>Yes, if QA signs off by Friday.</v>
```

A small parser that also merges consecutive cues from the same speaker:

```python
import re

CUE = re.compile(
    r"(\d{2}:\d{2}:\d{2}\.\d{3}) --> (\d{2}:\d{2}:\d{2}\.\d{3})\s*\n(.+?)(?:\n\n|\Z)",
    re.S,
)
VOICE = re.compile(r"<v ([^>]+)>(.*?)</v>", re.S)

def parse_teams_vtt(vtt: str):
    turns = []
    for start, end, body in CUE.findall(vtt):
        m = VOICE.search(body)
        speaker, text = (m.group(1), m.group(2)) if m else ("Unknown", body)
        text = " ".join(text.split())
        if turns and turns[-1]["speaker"] == speaker:
            turns[-1]["text"] += " " + text
            turns[-1]["end"] = end
        else:
            turns.append({"speaker": speaker, "start": start, "end": end, "text": text})
    return turns
```

Some cues may carry an identifier line before the timestamp; the regex above skips it because it only matches from the timestamp onwards.

## Step 4: Get notified instead of polling

Graph supports change notifications for transcripts. Subscribe to new transcripts for a specific meeting:

```
POST https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/subscriptions
{
  "changeType": "created",
  "notificationUrl": "https://your-app.example.com/graph/notify",
  "resource": "communications/onlineMeetings/{meetingId}/transcripts",
  "expirationDateTime": "2026-10-25T12:00:00Z",
  "clientState": "a-secret-you-verify"
}
```

There are also tenant-wide resources for transcripts (for example `communications/onlineMeetings/getAllTranscripts`), which need the application permission and are subject to Microsoft's licensing and metering rules for these APIs. Check current requirements before you design around them. Subscriptions expire, so renew them on a schedule, and always validate `clientState`.

## Step 5: Turn transcripts into something people read

Nobody reads raw transcripts. The usual next step is a short summary: decisions, action items with owners and dates, and open questions. If you're generating that with an LLM, feed it the parsed speaker turns (not the raw VTT) and give it a fixed output structure. A plain [meeting summary template](https://lynkk.ai/blog/meeting-summary-template) is a good target format, because humans already know how to read it.

## Limits of the native route

The Graph route is ideal for internal tools inside one Microsoft 365 tenant. It's a weaker fit when:

- you meet with external organizations whose meetings you don't own;
- you also meet on Zoom, Google Meet or in person;
- transcription isn't consistently turned on;
- you want features beyond the transcript, like search across months of meetings.

If you're weighing Copilot, Teams Premium recaps and third-party notetakers rather than building, the Lynkk team wrote a comparison of [AI note takers for Microsoft Teams](https://lynkk.ai/blog/ai-note-taker-microsoft-teams), with costs for a 10-person team. And Lynkk's own [Teams integration](https://lynkk.ai/integrations/microsoft-teams) records Teams calls with a bot, the Chrome extension or the Mac app, without depending on Teams transcription being on.

# Downloading Zoom Cloud Recording Transcripts With the Zoom API (and Parsing the VTT)

Zoom can generate an audio transcript for cloud recordings. Most people find it in the web portal and download it by hand. If you want those transcripts in your own system (a searchable archive, an internal summary bot, a data warehouse), the Zoom API gives you the same file programmatically.

This post covers authentication, finding the transcript file, parsing Zoom's VTT format and a webhook that delivers new transcripts as they're ready.

> **Prerequisites.** You need a Zoom plan with cloud recording, and the **audio transcript** option enabled in the account's recording settings. Local recordings don't produce cloud transcripts. If you're not sure which options your plan has, the non-technical guide to [transcribing Zoom meetings](https://lynkk.ai/blog/how-to-transcribe-zoom-meetings) covers the three ways, including on a free plan.

## Step 1: Create a Server-to-Server OAuth app

For an internal tool that reads your own account's recordings, a **Server-to-Server OAuth** app in the Zoom App Marketplace is the simplest option. Give it the cloud recording read scopes (Zoom's granular scopes for listing and reading recording files) and note the account ID, client ID and client secret.

```python
import base64, os, requests

def zoom_token() -> str:
    auth = base64.b64encode(
        f"{os.environ['ZOOM_CLIENT_ID']}:{os.environ['ZOOM_CLIENT_SECRET']}".encode()
    ).decode()
    r = requests.post(
        "https://zoom.us/oauth/token",
        params={"grant_type": "account_credentials",
                "account_id": os.environ["ZOOM_ACCOUNT_ID"]},
        headers={"Authorization": f"Basic {auth}"},
        timeout=20,
    )
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()["access_token"]   # valid for about an hour; cache it
```

## Step 2: Find the transcript file

Each meeting's cloud recording has several files: video, audio, chat and, if enabled, a transcript. List them and pick the one with `file_type == "TRANSCRIPT"`:

```python
API = "https://api.zoom.us/v2"

def transcript_download_url(token: str, meeting_id: str) -> str | None:
    r = requests.get(f"{API}/meetings/{meeting_id}/recordings",
                     headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}"}, timeout=20)
    r.raise_for_status()
    for f in r.json().get("recording_files", []):
        if f.get("file_type") == "TRANSCRIPT" and f.get("status") == "completed":
            return f["download_url"]
    return None
```

For recurring meetings, the meeting ID refers to the series. Use the specific occurrence's UUID to get one instance; UUIDs that start with `/` or contain `//` must be **double URL-encoded** in the path, a classic Zoom API gotcha.

To list everything recorded in a date range, use `GET /users/me/recordings?from=YYYY-MM-DD&to=YYYY-MM-DD` and page through `next_page_token`.

## Step 3: Download and parse

```python
def download(url: str, token: str) -> str:
    r = requests.get(url, headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}"},
                     timeout=60, allow_redirects=True)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.content.decode("utf-8")
```

Zoom's transcript VTT puts the speaker name at the start of the cue text:

```
WEBVTT

1
00:00:02.120 --> 00:00:05.480
Priya Shah: Can we move the rollout to the 28th?

2
00:00:06.010 --> 00:00:08.300
Dev Patel: Yes, if QA signs off by Friday.
```

That's different from Teams, which uses `<v Speaker>` tags. A parser for Zoom's format:

```python
import re

CUE = re.compile(
    r"(?:^\d+\s*\n)?(\d{2}:\d{2}:\d{2}\.\d{3}) --> (\d{2}:\d{2}:\d{2}\.\d{3})\s*\n(.+?)(?=\n\s*\n|\Z)",
    re.S | re.M,
)

def parse_zoom_vtt(vtt: str):
    turns = []
    for start, end, body in CUE.findall(vtt):
        body = " ".join(body.split())
        speaker, sep, text = body.partition(": ")
        if not sep:                      # no speaker prefix on this cue
            speaker, text = "Unknown", body
        if turns and turns[-1]["speaker"] == speaker:
            turns[-1]["text"] += " " + text
            turns[-1]["end"] = end
        else:
            turns.append({"speaker": speaker, "start": start, "end": end, "text": text})
    return turns
```

Speaker names come from participants' Zoom display names, so "iPhone" or "Conference Room 3" will show up exactly like that. Plan for a rename step.

## Step 4: Get transcripts automatically with a webhook

Polling works, but Zoom can tell you when a transcript is ready. Subscribe your app to the **`recording.transcript_completed`** event. Zoom first sends a URL validation challenge, then signs each event so you can verify it:

```python
import hashlib, hmac, json, time
from flask import Flask, request, jsonify

app = Flask(__name__)
SECRET = os.environ["ZOOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET"].encode()

@app.post("/zoom/webhook")
def webhook():
    body = request.get_data(as_text=True)
    event = json.loads(body)

    if event.get("event") == "endpoint.url_validation":
        plain = event["payload"]["plainToken"]
        enc = hmac.new(SECRET, plain.encode(), hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
        return jsonify(plainToken=plain, encryptedToken=enc)

    ts = request.headers.get("x-zm-request-timestamp", "")
    sig = request.headers.get("x-zm-signature", "")
    expected = "v0=" + hmac.new(SECRET, f"v0:{ts}:{body}".encode(), hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
    if not hmac.compare_digest(sig, expected) or abs(time.time() - int(ts or 0)) > 300:
        return "", 401

    if event["event"] == "recording.transcript_completed":
        enqueue_transcript_job(event["payload"]["object"])   # fetch + parse async
    return "", 200
```

Do the download in a background job. Webhook handlers should return quickly.

## What you get, and what you don't

This pipeline gets you Zoom's transcript, reliably and automatically, for meetings recorded to your own account's cloud. It doesn't cover:

- meetings hosted by **other organizations** (you don't own their recordings);
- meetings that weren't **cloud recorded**;
- Google Meet, Teams or **in-person** conversations;
- summaries, action items and cross-meeting search.

That's the space notetakers occupy, with a bot in the call, a desktop app or the platform's own AI Companion. If you're comparing those rather than building, here's a rundown of [Zoom note takers](https://lynkk.ai/blog/zoom-note-taker), from AI Companion to bot-free apps. Lynkk's [Zoom integration](https://lynkk.ai/integrations/zoom) is one example: it records Zoom with a bot, the Mac app or the Chrome extension, without needing cloud recording turned on.

# Zoom AI Companion Gave Us Summaries. Our CRM Stayed Empty.

*A summary is not a record. Why sales teams still retype every call, and three ways to close the gap.*

Hi, and welcome to **After the Call**, a newsletter from the Lynkk team about what happens after meetings end: the notes, the follow-ups and the work that falls through the cracks.

This week's issue starts with a question someone typed into Google, almost word for word:

> "Zoom AI Companion gives us summaries but nothing in our CRM. What other tools could close that gap for reps?"

It's a very specific complaint, and a very common one. Let's unpack it.

## The summary arrived. Then what?

Zoom AI Companion (on the paid Zoom plans that include it) does a decent job of writing a meeting summary. The rep gets an email or a doc. It's readable. It's even accurate.

And then the rep opens Salesforce or HubSpot and types the same information again: next steps, budget, timeline, who the decision maker is. Or, more often, doesn't.

The problem isn't the summary's quality. It's that **a summary is written for a human to read, and a CRM record is structured for a system to use.** They're different shapes.

A summary says: *"Priya mentioned that their budget has grown since discovery and they want to start with a smaller group."*

A CRM needs: *Budget: $50K. Pilot size: 15. Next step: security review. Decision maker: IT lead (not yet named).*

Converting one into the other is exactly the admin reps hate most, so it's exactly what gets skipped.

## Three gaps, not one

When teams say "nothing gets into our CRM," they usually mean one of three different things:

**1. Structure.** The notes don't separate budget, timeline, stakeholders and next steps. Fix: use a note format built for sales calls, with fixed sections.

**2. Transport.** The structured notes exist but live in a different app. Fix: a real CRM sync, or a one-click copy into the right fields.

**3. Coverage.** Half the calls aren't on Zoom. They're on Teams, Google Meet, a phone, or in person at the customer's office. Fix: a tool that captures every channel your reps actually sell through.

The second searcher's version of the question shows the third gap clearly: *"alternatives to Zoom AI Companion for sales reps who also take customer calls on Teams and Google Meet."*

## What to look for in a replacement (or a supplement)

If you're evaluating tools to close this gap, ask:

- **Does it write sales-shaped notes?** Look for sections like customer, stakeholders, pain points, budget and next steps, not just "summary".
- **What exactly does "CRM integration" mean?** Automatic field sync, a push button, or "copy to clipboard"? All three exist, and vendors use the same word for all three. Ask for a demo of the actual workflow.
- **Does it cover every call type your reps use?** Zoom, Teams, Meet and in-person, in one archive.
- **Can reps ask questions across past calls?** "What did Acme say about pricing in Q2?" is the question that prepares a rep for a renewal.

We wrote a longer comparison of [Zoom AI Companion alternatives](https://lynkk.ai/blog/zoom-ai-companion-alternatives), with pricing and bot or bot-free capture for each.

A note on honesty, since we make one of these tools: **Lynkk doesn't sync to CRMs yet.** On Pro, its Sales Call summary shape writes notes with customer, stakeholders, pain points and budget sections that a rep can copy into Salesforce or HubSpot, and on every plan it records Zoom, Meet, Teams and in-person calls and sends action items to Jira. If automatic field sync is your must-have, test the tools that offer it, and check that the sync does what the demo shows.

## The bigger idea: conversation intelligence

Zoom's summaries are one step on a longer path. Larger sales teams often move to "conversation intelligence" platforms that analyze calls across the whole pipeline: talk ratios, competitor mentions, deal risk. Those are powerful and expensive, and many small teams don't need all of it. Here's a plain-English overview of [conversation intelligence for sales teams](https://lynkk.ai/blog/sales-conversation-intelligence), including when it's worth it and when a good notetaker is enough.

## The fastest fix you can make today

While you're evaluating tools, there's one change that helps immediately: **send a structured follow-up email after every customer call, and paste it into the CRM.**

Five lines: what we agreed, what you'll do, what we'll do, the date, and one open question. The customer gets clarity, the rep gets a record, and the CRM gets *something*. If you need templates, here are [12 follow-up email examples](https://lynkk.ai/blog/follow-up-email-after-meeting) for sales, client and internal calls.

## This week's takeaway

The gap between "AI summarized the call" and "the CRM knows what happened" is structure plus transport plus coverage. Most tools solve one. Ask which ones yours solves.

Thanks for reading. If someone forwarded this to you, you can subscribe below to get the next issue. And if you have a meeting problem you'd like us to write about, just reply.

*The Lynkk team*

# BANT Isn't Dead. It's Just Badly Written Down.

*The world's most criticized qualification framework fails less in the call than in the notes afterwards.*

Welcome back to **After the Call**. This week: a sales framework that's been declared dead more times than we can count, and why the funeral might be premature.

## The case against BANT

BANT stands for **Budget, Authority, Need and Timeline**. IBM popularized it decades ago, and every few years someone writes a post explaining why it no longer works. The arguments are familiar:

- Buyers don't know their budget early on.
- "Authority" is now a committee, not a person.
- Asking "do you have budget?" in the first call feels like an interrogation.
- It's seller-centered rather than buyer-centered.

All fair. But notice what these criticisms are about: **how the questions are asked.** Almost none of them say the four things BANT tracks don't matter. Budget, decision-makers, need and timing still decide whether deals close.

## Where BANT really fails

Here's a pattern that's easy to recognize once you look for it: BANT often breaks down after the call, not during it.

A rep asks good questions. The customer gives a nuanced answer: *"We've set aside something like thirty for this, but honestly if the pilot goes well, finance said they'd look at more."* The rep writes "Budget: ✓" in the CRM.

Three weeks later, the deal stalls on price, and nobody remembers that the budget was conditional on the pilot.

That's the real BANT failure mode: **compressing rich answers into checkboxes.** "Authority: yes" hides the fact that IT has a veto. "Timeline: Q1" hides that Q1 depends on a reorganization. The framework asked the right questions. The notes threw away the answers.

## Writing BANT down properly

Here's a simple rule that fixes most of it: **for each letter, write down the customer's words, not your verdict.**

| Letter | Checkbox version | Better version |
|---|---|---|
| Budget | ✓ | "Around $30K set aside; more possible if pilot succeeds (Priya, discovery call)" |
| Authority | VP Eng | "Priya owns evaluation; IT must sign off security review before rollout" |
| Need | Context loss | "Reps rebuild each account from scratch between calls" |
| Timeline | Q1 | "Pilot after IT review; no hard date yet" |

The better version takes 30 extra seconds and saves the deal review a week later. It also tells your manager what you actually know versus what you're assuming.

If you want the full breakdown (what each letter means, the questions that get honest answers, and where BANT really does fall short), we wrote a detailed guide to [BANT sales qualification](https://lynkk.ai/blog/bant-sales-qualification).

## Let the recording do the remembering

The reason reps compress answers into checkboxes is simple: they're writing from memory, after the call, between two other calls. Memory compresses automatically.

Recording the call (with the customer's consent) changes that. The exact words are captured. A good note format then pulls budget, stakeholders, pain points and next steps into separate sections, each tied to the moment it was said. The rep's job becomes checking the notes, not writing them.

That's the workflow behind most modern [sales call notetakers](https://lynkk.ai/use-cases/sales-calls), including ours (in Lynkk, the sales-call sections come from the Sales Call summary shape on Pro).

## BANT is best used before the next call

The most underrated use of BANT notes isn't qualification. It's preparation.

Before your second call with a prospect, read your BANT notes and ask: what don't we know yet? If Authority says "IT must sign off," your next call should include a question about the IT review. If Budget says "more possible if pilot succeeds," you know what the pilot has to prove.

Five minutes of prep with good notes beats thirty minutes of rapport-building with bad ones. We wrote up a short [meeting preparation checklist](https://lynkk.ai/blog/meeting-preparation) built around this idea.

## This week's takeaway

BANT doesn't fail because the letters are wrong. It fails because the answers get reduced to ticks. Write down the customer's words, and the old framework starts working again.

Thanks for reading. If this was useful, forward it to the person on your team who owns the CRM. They'll appreciate it.

*The Lynkk team*

# What Gong Costs, and What a 10-Person Sales Team Actually Needs

*Conversation intelligence was built for big revenue teams. If you're small, start with the problem, not the platform.*

Welcome back to **After the Call**. This week we're talking about money: specifically, the moment a growing sales team decides it needs "something like Gong."

## The question behind the question

When a founder or first sales leader asks "how much does Gong cost?", they're rarely just asking about price. They're asking: *Do we need this yet? What would we get? What would we miss without it?*

Price is the easy part to research and the hard part to pin down, because Gong doesn't publish its pricing. Deals are negotiated, and reported figures typically involve a per-user license plus a platform fee, often on annual contracts. We pulled together what's publicly reported in [what Gong costs in 2026](https://lynkk.ai/blog/gong-pricing), including what that tends to mean for a 10-person team. Treat any figure you see (including ours) as an estimate, and get a quote.

The more useful question is what problem you're trying to solve.

## What conversation intelligence platforms actually do

Platforms like Gong do several jobs at once:

1. **Record and transcribe** sales calls.
2. **Summarize** them and extract next steps.
3. **Analyze patterns** across many calls: talk-to-listen ratios, competitor mentions, objections, topics that correlate with won deals.
4. **Coach**: managers review calls, leave comments, build libraries of good examples.
5. **Forecast and manage deals**: flag risk based on activity and what was said.

Jobs 1 and 2 are now available in many tools at a fraction of the price. Jobs 3 to 5 are where platforms earn their cost, and they get more valuable the more calls and reps you have. Pattern analysis on 40 calls a month says less than on 4,000.

For a fuller picture of the category, here's our overview of [conversation intelligence for sales teams](https://lynkk.ai/blog/sales-conversation-intelligence), from call prep to follow-up.

## What a 10-person team usually needs

At around ten reps, the biggest problems tend to be surprisingly basic:

- **Context lost between calls.** The rep can't remember what the customer said three weeks ago.
- **Handoffs fail.** An SDR's discovery notes don't reach the AE; the AE's promises don't reach customer success.
- **Managers can't see deals.** Pipeline reviews depend on the rep's memory and optimism.
- **The CRM is stale.** Nobody wants to type notes after every call.

None of these require pattern analysis across thousands of calls. They require **every call to be captured, structured and searchable**, so anyone on the team can find what the customer said.

## A simple way to decide

Ask yourself three questions:

**1. Is your biggest problem memory or method?**
If reps forget what customers said, you need capture and search. If reps remember perfectly but don't know how to handle objections, you need coaching. Coaching is where full platforms shine.

**2. How many calls do you record a month?**
Below a few hundred, pattern analytics tend to be noisy. Above a few thousand, they start telling you things you didn't know.

**3. Who will use the insights?**
If nobody has time to review dashboards, you're paying for reports nobody reads.

If your answers are "memory," "not many yet" and "the reps themselves," start with a notetaker that captures every call and lets reps ask questions across past calls. Upgrade to a full platform when you have the volume and a manager with time to coach.

If you want a direct side-by-side, we keep a [Lynkk vs Gong comparison](https://lynkk.ai/compare/gong) page. It's written by us, so read it as a vendor's view, and check the points that matter to you in a trial.

## This week's takeaway

Buy for the problem you have now, not the one you'll have at 50 reps. For most small teams, that problem is memory, and memory is cheap to fix.

Thanks for reading. Got a "should we buy X" question you're stuck on? Reply and tell us. We might cover it in a future issue.

# Hinglish Is How India Actually Meets. Most Meeting Tools Still Pretend It Isn't.

*Half your sentence in Hindi, half in English, and a transcript that makes sense of neither.*

Namaste, and welcome back to **After the Call**. This week's issue is for everyone who has ever read an AI meeting summary and wondered which meeting it was describing.

## The sentence every Indian team says

> "Client ne bola ki budget thoda tight hai, so let's propose the smaller pilot first."

If you work in an Indian company, you've heard (and said) a hundred sentences like that this week. Hindi grammar, English nouns, a switch in the middle. Linguists call it *code-switching*. Everyone else calls it Hinglish, or just "how we talk."

Now run that sentence through a meeting tool that asks you to choose a language up front. Choose English, and "client ne bola ki budget thoda tight hai" becomes a string of near-miss English words. Choose Hindi, and "propose the smaller pilot" comes out as an awkward transliteration. Either way, the one line that mattered in the meeting is garbled.

## Why it matters more than accuracy scores suggest

A transcript with a few wrong words isn't a disaster. A transcript where the *important* words are wrong is.

In Hinglish meetings, the important words are very often the English ones: product names, numbers, deadlines, client names, technical terms. "Deployment," "pilot," "28 tareekh tak," "sign off." If a tool mangles exactly those, the summary built on top of it will be confidently wrong, and the action items will name the wrong thing.

## Three things to check before you trust a tool

**1. Does it handle mixed speech in one recording?**
Not "does it support Hindi" and "does it support English" separately. Ask whether it handles both *in the same sentence*. Then test it.

**2. What script does the transcript come out in?**
Devanagari, Roman script or a mix? There's no wrong answer, but it should match how your team reads and searches. Most people search their notes in Roman script, so a pure-Devanagari transcript can be hard to search even if it's accurate.

**3. Test with your own audio.**
Record a real 10-minute team meeting (with everyone's okay), run it through each tool you're considering, and read the summaries side by side. Look at names, numbers and deadlines first.

## The free options are better than you think

If you mainly need Hindi (rather than mixed) transcription, there are surprisingly good free options: Google Docs voice typing, YouTube's automatic captions for uploaded videos, and the dictation built into phones. We wrote a practical guide to [Hindi transcription in India](https://lynkk.ai/blog/hindi-transcription), with free tools, Hinglish meetings and tips for better accuracy.

If your meetings run on Google Meet, the question gets more specific: does Gemini's note-taking work for your language mix, and if not, what does? We compared [Google Meet AI note takers for Indian teams](https://lynkk.ai/blog/google-meet-ai-note-taker), including Hindi and Hinglish support and free plans.

## Where we stand (a short disclosure)

# The Follow-Up Email Is the Meeting

*Forty-five minutes of conversation, and the only part anyone will remember is the five lines you send afterwards.*

Welcome back to **After the Call**. This week's issue is about the most underrated document in business: the email you send after a meeting.

## Memory is a terrible record

Here's what happens after almost every meeting. Everyone leaves with a slightly different version of what was agreed. The differences are small: a date that was "end of the month" for one person and "the 28th" for another, a deliverable that was "a draft" or "the final version." Over a week, small differences become missed deadlines and awkward conversations.

The follow-up email fixes that. Not because it's polite (though it is), but because it's the first time the meeting's outcome exists in writing. **Until someone writes it down, the meeting didn't decide anything. It just talked.**

## The five-line follow-up

You don't need a long email. You need five things:

1. **What we decided.** One or two sentences.
2. **What I'll do, and by when.**
3. **What you'll do, and by when.**
4. **The next touchpoint.** A date, a meeting, a milestone.
5. **One open question**, if there is one.

That's it. Here's what it looks like:

> Hi Priya,
>
> Thanks for today. To confirm: we'll start with a 15-person pilot once your IT team completes the security review.
>
> I'll send the security overview and the pilot plan by Friday. Could you introduce us to your IT lead this week?
>
> Let's check in on the 3rd to confirm the pilot start date.
>
> One open question: who on your side will own training for the pilot group?

Short enough to write in three minutes. Specific enough that nobody can misremember it.

For different situations (a client meeting, a networking coffee, a sales call, the "they never replied" follow-up), we put together [12 follow-up email examples](https://lynkk.ai/blog/follow-up-email-after-meeting) with subject lines and timing advice.

## Internal meetings need it too

The follow-up isn't just for clients. Internal meetings drift even more, because everyone assumes someone else will send the recap.

For team meetings, the format shifts slightly toward a summary: decisions, action items with owners and dates, and open questions, posted where the team will see it. A consistent format matters more than a perfect one; people learn where to look. Here's a free [meeting summary template](https://lynkk.ai/blog/meeting-summary-template) with real examples for team, client and project meetings.

## Send it within the hour

Timing matters more than polish. A follow-up sent within an hour:

- catches mistakes while everyone still remembers the meeting;
- signals that you were listening;
- lands before the other person's next meeting buries this one.

A follow-up sent three days later is a history lesson.

If you struggle to find the time, there are two tricks. First, write the email *during* the last five minutes of the meeting, and read it out loud: "Here's what I'm going to send, anything missing?" Second, let a notetaker draft it. Many tools, ours included, write the [meeting notes](https://lynkk.ai/features/meeting-notes) (decisions, action items with owners and due dates) after the call and email you the summary, so the follow-up becomes a two-minute edit instead of a ten-minute write.

## The hidden benefit: your future self

There's one more reason to send the follow-up, and it's selfish. Six months from now, when someone asks "didn't we agree to X?", the answer will be in your sent folder, dated, in writing, with the other person's reply below it.

That's worth five lines.

## This week's takeaway

The meeting isn't over until the follow-up is sent. Five lines, within the hour, every time.

Thanks for reading. If you have a favorite follow-up line or template, hit reply and share it. We'll collect the best ones in a future issue.

# Board Meetings: The Agenda Is Easy. The Minutes Are Hard.

*Founders spend days on the board deck and minutes on the minutes. That's backwards.*

Welcome back to **After the Call**. This week's issue is for founders, executive directors and anyone who has ever been told "you'll need to take the minutes" five minutes before a board meeting.

*A quick note: this is general information, not legal advice. Requirements for board minutes depend on your jurisdiction, your entity type and your bylaws. If in doubt, ask your company lawyer or secretary.*

## The agenda gets all the attention

Most of the energy before a board meeting goes into the deck: metrics, narrative, the ask. The agenda is usually a copy of last quarter's with dates changed. That's fine. Board agendas are fairly standard: call to order, approval of the previous minutes, reports, old business, new business, any votes, adjournment.

If you need a starting point, we published a [board meeting agenda template](https://lynkk.ai/blog/board-meeting-agenda) for US boards, with startup and nonprofit samples and how consent agendas work.

The minutes get almost none of that attention. Someone types notes during the meeting, cleans them up a week later, and they're approved at the next meeting without much reading.

## Why the minutes matter more than the deck

The deck is forgotten within a quarter. The minutes are permanent.

Board minutes are the official record of what the board decided: approvals of option grants, financings, budgets, officer appointments, major contracts. They're what lawyers, auditors and future investors look at during due diligence. When a question comes up years later ("did the board actually approve that grant?"), the minutes are the answer.

Badly kept minutes create real problems: missing approvals that have to be ratified later, unclear records of who voted how, and in some cases, discussions recorded in more detail than anyone wanted.

## Notes are not minutes

The most common mistake is treating minutes as detailed notes. They're not. Minutes record **what the board did**, not everything the board said.

Typically, minutes include:

- the date, time and place, and whether it was in person or virtual;
- who attended (directors, observers, guests) and whether a quorum was present;
- approval of the previous meeting's minutes;
- each motion, who made and seconded it, and the outcome of the vote;
- any director who abstained or recused themselves;
- the time of adjournment.

They usually *don't* include a transcript of the debate. Many lawyers advise keeping discussion summaries short and factual. We wrote a longer explainer on [meeting notes vs minutes](https://lynkk.ai/blog/meeting-notes-vs-minutes) and how to turn one into the other.

## A practical routine

Here's a routine that works for most early-stage boards:

1. **Assign a secretary** before the meeting. Not the person presenting. Often a company lawyer, the COO or a designated staff member.
2. **Prepare a minutes skeleton** from the agenda: every item and every expected vote already listed, with blanks for outcomes.
3. **Capture the meeting** (with the board's agreement), whether by careful notes or a recording, so the secretary can focus on motions and votes rather than typing everything.
4. **Draft the minutes within 48 hours**, while memories are fresh. Use the skeleton, fill in outcomes, keep discussion summaries brief.
5. **Have counsel review** anything involving equity, financing or conflicts of interest.
6. **Circulate the draft** with the next meeting's materials and approve it as the first item of business.

If you've never seen good minutes, start from a real [meeting minutes sample](https://lynkk.ai/blog/meeting-minutes-sample) for team and board meetings, then adapt it to your bylaws.

## Should you record board meetings?

This is a genuine judgment call, and boards disagree. A recording makes drafting accurate minutes much easier. It also creates a verbatim record that may be discoverable, and some directors speak less freely when recorded.

Common approaches: record only to assist drafting and delete the recording once minutes are approved; record but keep it with counsel; or don't record at all and rely on a skilled secretary. Whatever you choose, decide it as a board, write the policy down, and tell everyone at the start of each meeting.

## This week's takeaway

Spend less time polishing the board deck and more time on the minutes. The deck persuades the board for an hour. The minutes speak for the board for years.

Thanks for reading. If you're a founder preparing for your first board meeting, forward this to whoever's taking the minutes.

# The One-on-One Is Where Managers Lose the Thread

*Your report remembers exactly what they told you last time. Do you?*

Welcome back to **After the Call**. This week is for managers, especially new ones, and especially anyone managing more than five people.

## The asymmetry nobody talks about

A one-on-one has two people in it, and they experience it very differently.

For your report, it's *the* meeting. It's the one time each week or fortnight where they get your full attention. They think about it in advance. They remember what they raised.

For you, it's one of seven one-on-ones this week, wedged between a planning meeting and a customer call. You walk in having forgotten that last time they mentioned feeling stretched, or that you promised to look into their training budget.

They notice. Not every time, but often enough. And each time, they learn a little lesson: *what I say here doesn't stick.*

## What gets lost

The things that slip between one-on-ones are rarely the big topics. They're the small signals:

- "I'm fine, just a bit tired with the launch."
- "I'd love to do more customer-facing work at some point."
- "The handoff with design has been a bit rough."
- Your own promise: "Let me check whether we can fund that course."

Each one is a thread. Pick it up next time and you build trust. Drop it and you lose a little.

## A note-taking habit that takes three minutes

You don't need a system. You need three minutes, twice:

**After the one-on-one (90 seconds):**
- What did they raise?
- What did I commit to?
- Anything I should watch for?

**Before the next one (90 seconds):**
- Reread the notes.
- Check your commitments. Did you do them?
- Pick one thing from last time to ask about first.

Opening with "Last time you mentioned the handoff with design was rough. How's that been?" is one of the most powerful sentences a manager can say. It costs nothing and it tells your report you were listening.

We wrote a full guide to [running one-on-one meetings](https://lynkk.ai/blog/one-on-one-meeting), with 20 questions, a sample agenda and a notes template you can copy.

## Should you record one-on-ones?

This is sensitive, and the honest answer is: *only if your report genuinely wants it.*

Some people love having a record. They can revisit feedback, and it removes any doubt about what was agreed. Others find a recording inhibiting, especially for conversations about stress, career worries or conflict with colleagues. A one-on-one where your report self-censors is worse than one with no notes at all.

If you do record:

- ask first, every time, and make "no" an easy answer;
- keep the notes private between the two of you;
- never use a recording of a one-on-one in a performance process without explicit agreement.

For managers who want help remembering without the weight of a recording, the three-minute written habit above is enough. For those whose reports prefer a record, tools exist that keep [one-on-one notes](https://lynkk.ai/use-cases/one-on-one-meetings) private to the people involved.

## The compound effect

Here's what happens after a few months of this habit. Your one-on-ones start with continuity instead of catch-up. Your reports bring better topics, because they trust they'll be followed up. Small problems surface earlier, because people mention them when they're still small.

None of it requires a framework. It requires remembering, and remembering requires writing things down. The same principle applies to any recurring meeting; there's a short [meeting preparation checklist](https://lynkk.ai/blog/meeting-preparation) that generalizes it.

## This week's takeaway

Before your next one-on-one, spend 90 seconds rereading what your report said last time. Then ask about it first.

Thanks for reading. If you're a manager with a one-on-one ritual that works, reply and tell us about it.

# Recruiters: The Interview Debrief Starts Before the Interview Ends

*Most hiring mistakes aren't made in the interview. They're made in the debrief, from memory, three days later.*

Welcome back to **After the Call**. This week's issue is for recruiters, hiring managers and anyone who has sat in a debrief thinking, "wait, which candidate said that?"

## The debrief problem

Picture a typical hiring loop. A candidate meets four interviewers over a day. Each interviewer has three other loops that week. The debrief happens on Thursday.

By Thursday, here's what each interviewer remembers: a general impression, one or two vivid moments, and the scorecard they filled in (if they filled it in right away, which many didn't).

The debrief then becomes a contest of impressions. The most confident voice in the room wins. Specific evidence, like what the candidate actually said about their last project, is mostly gone.

That's how good candidates get rejected for "not seeming senior enough" and weaker ones get hired because they were memorable.

## Evidence beats impressions

Structured interviewing research has argued for years that consistent questions and evidence-based scoring predict job performance better than unstructured conversations and gut feel. The practical side of that is simple: **write down what the candidate said, not what you thought of it.**

"Strong on system design" is an impression.
"Described splitting a monolith into three services; explained the data migration plan and the rollback strategy" is evidence.

Evidence is what makes a debrief fair, and it's what lets an interviewer who disagrees point at something concrete.

## Three ways to capture evidence

**1. Take verbatim notes during the interview.** Effective but exhausting, and it splits your attention. Candidates notice when you're typing more than listening.

**2. Write a structured scorecard right after.** Ten minutes, immediately, before the next meeting. Works well if interviewers actually do it, and it's the minimum every team should require.

**3. Record and transcribe (with consent).** The interviewer listens fully, and the transcript provides the evidence. The scorecard is then written from the transcript, quoting the candidate's words.

Option 3 is increasingly common. If you go that way, a few rules:

- **Tell candidates in advance** that interviews are recorded, explain why (fairness and accuracy), and offer a way to opt out without penalty.
- **Check local law.** Recording consent rules vary by country and state.
- **Limit access** to the hiring team, and set a retention period. Don't keep recordings of rejected candidates forever.

We wrote a practical guide to [interview transcription for recruiters](https://lynkk.ai/blog/recruiting-interview-transcription), with an example transcript and how teams turn transcripts into faster debriefs. If you have existing recordings to transcribe, here's a general guide to [transcribing audio to text](https://lynkk.ai/blog/transcribe-audio-to-text), from free built-in options to paid tools.

## A better debrief format

Whatever capture method you use, the debrief itself improves with structure:

1. **Scorecards submitted before the debrief**, so nobody anchors on the first opinion voiced.
2. **Each interviewer shares evidence, then a score**, in that order.
3. **Disagreements are resolved by evidence**: "What did they say that made you rate them a 2?"
4. **The decision and its reasons are written down**, so the next loop for the same role can learn from it.

A consistent written summary for each candidate (strengths with evidence, concerns with evidence, decision, next step) works much like any good [meeting summary](https://lynkk.ai/blog/meeting-summary-template). The structure is the point.

## This week's takeaway

The debrief is only as good as the evidence that reaches it. Capture what candidates said, while they're saying it or immediately after, and your hiring decisions get fairer and faster.

Thanks for reading. If you run a recruiting team and have a debrief format you swear by, reply and tell us. We'd love to feature a few.

# Lawyers, Doctors and the Limits of AI Transcription

*AI transcripts are good enough for most meetings. In law and medicine, "most" isn't the standard.*

Welcome back to **After the Call**. This week we're stepping into two professions where a transcript isn't just a convenience. It can be evidence, or part of a medical record.

*This issue is general information, not legal or medical compliance advice. Requirements differ by jurisdiction and by organization. Check with your compliance team or counsel before changing how you record.*

## Two kinds of transcript

It helps to separate two very different uses.

**Working transcripts** help professionals do their job: notes from a client intake call, a case strategy meeting, a clinical team huddle, a call with opposing counsel's office about scheduling. Accuracy matters, but a few errors are tolerable, because a human reads and uses the notes.

**Record transcripts** become part of an official record: court proceedings, depositions, sworn statements, a patient's medical record, documentation that supports billing. Here accuracy, formatting and chain of custody can be legal requirements.

AI is now genuinely useful for the first kind. For the second, the question is much harder.

## In law

For depositions and court proceedings, formal transcripts are generally produced by certified court reporters or official transcription processes, following specific formatting and certification rules. An AI-generated transcript isn't a substitute for those.

Where AI fits well in a law firm:

- **Client meetings and intake calls**, so the lawyer can focus on the client instead of typing;
- **Internal case strategy meetings**, where decisions and tasks need to be captured;
- **Reviewing long recordings** (interviews, hearings you have audio of) to find relevant passages quickly, with a human verifying anything you'll rely on.

The big caveats are privilege and confidentiality. Before using any AI tool on client conversations, a firm should know where the data goes, who can access it, whether the vendor trains models on it, and how long it's kept.

We wrote a longer piece on [legal transcription services vs AI](https://lynkk.ai/blog/legal-transcription-service): what services cost, when AI is enough, and when you still need a human service. For firms looking at meeting notes specifically, there's an overview of how [lawyers use Lynkk](https://lynkk.ai/use-cases/lawyers) for client and internal meetings.

## In medicine

Clinical documentation is a heavy burden, and AI scribes and dictation tools have become popular for good reason. But healthcare adds strict requirements:

- In the US, tools that handle protected health information typically need to meet HIPAA requirements, which usually includes the vendor signing a **business associate agreement (BAA)**.
- Clinical notes become part of the medical record, so errors carry real risk.
- Medical vocabulary (drug names, dosages, anatomy) is where general-purpose transcription makes the most dangerous mistakes.

A general meeting notetaker isn't automatically suitable for clinical use, even if its transcripts are accurate. The questions to ask are about compliance and workflow, not just accuracy. Here's our guide to [medical transcription software and AI dictation](https://lynkk.ai/blog/medical-transcription-software), including what a HIPAA-compliant AI note taker needs and the categories of tools clinicians use.

Being straightforward about our own product: Lynkk suits care-team huddles, case reviews and admin meetings, not clinical charting. It doesn't offer a region setting for where data is processed today (processing may happen in countries including India and the United States), and it isn't end-to-end encrypted, because it has to read a recording to transcribe it. If you work in healthcare, get a signed BAA before any patient information goes into any AI tool, Lynkk included, and use tools designed and contracted for charting.

## The checklist for any regulated profession

Before using an AI transcription tool, ask the vendor, in writing:

1. Do you train models on our data?
2. Which third parties process our audio and transcripts?
3. Where is data processed and stored? Can we choose?
4. Will you sign the agreements our profession requires (for example a BAA)?
5. Who inside our organization can access a recording or transcript, and is access logged?
6. How do we delete data, and how quickly is it gone?

If the answers are vague, the tool isn't ready for your sensitive work, however good the transcripts are.

## This week's takeaway

AI transcription is excellent for working notes and still not a replacement for official records. Know which kind of transcript you're creating before you choose the tool.

Thanks for reading. If you work in law or healthcare and have found a workflow that balances efficiency and compliance, we'd love to hear about it. Just reply.

# Read AI, Otter, Copilot or None of the Above? A Letter to Someone Choosing a Note Taker

*You don't need the best AI note taker. You need the one your team will still be using in three months.*

Welcome back to **After the Call**. This week's issue is written as a letter, because it answers a question that comes up constantly: *"We're choosing a note taker. Which one should we pick?"*

The usual disclosure, louder than usual: we make one of these tools. So we'll try hard to give you a way of deciding rather than a sales pitch.

---

Dear person with twelve browser tabs of comparison posts open,

First, close most of them. They mostly compare the same features in different orders, and most were written by a vendor (including ours). They won't tell you what you actually need to know: which tool fits the way *your* team meets.

Here's how we'd decide.

## Start with what you already pay for

Before adding anything, check what your meeting platform already includes.

- **On Microsoft Teams?** Depending on your licenses, you may already have transcription, intelligent recap with Teams Premium, or Copilot. They're often the simplest option, and the most limited outside Teams. We wrote a breakdown of [AI note takers for Microsoft Teams](https://lynkk.ai/blog/ai-note-taker-microsoft-teams), including what Copilot and Teams Premium cost for a 10-person team.
- **On Zoom?** Zoom AI Companion is included with many paid plans.
- **On Google Meet?** Gemini's note-taking may be included with your Workspace plan.

If your team meets on one platform and the built-in option is included, try it properly for two weeks before buying anything. It may be enough.

## If it isn't enough, ask why

The reasons built-in tools fall short are usually specific:

- you meet across two or three platforms;
- you also meet in person;
- you speak more than one language in the same meeting;
- you want action items in your task tracker, or questions answered across months of meetings;
- you need features the built-in plan doesn't include.

Write down your reason. It's your filter.

## The popular names, briefly

You've probably narrowed it to a few well-known tools. Two that come up constantly are Otter and Read AI. They take different approaches: broadly, Otter grew out of transcription and is known for live transcripts, while Read AI leans into meeting analytics and reports. Which matters more depends on whether you care most about the transcript or the insights. We put them [head to head, Read AI vs Otter AI](https://lynkk.ai/blog/read-ai-vs-otter-ai), on free limits, price per user and integrations for US teams.

If you're already using Otter and something isn't working, start from what's missing. Here's a comparison of [Otter.ai alternatives](https://lynkk.ai/blog/otter-ai-alternatives) by use case: sales, product and in-person meetings.

## Use the free plans as a trial

Nearly every tool has a free plan, and they're wildly different. Some cap meetings, some cap minutes, some cap how long notes are kept, some cap AI summaries. Match the cap to your habits: lots of short meetings, or a few long ones? Here's a side-by-side of [free AI note taker plans](https://lynkk.ai/blog/best-free-ai-note-takers) and what each upgrade costs.

Then do the one thing almost nobody does: **pick two tools and run both on the same real meetings for a week.** Compare the notes. Which got the names right? Which caught the action items? Which one did your colleagues actually open?

## The question that decides it

After the trial, ask your team one question: *"Which one would you be annoyed to lose?"*

That's your answer. Not the feature list. Not the price difference of a few dollars. The tool people would miss is the one they're actually using, and a note taker nobody uses is the most expensive one of all.

Warmly,
*The Lynkk team*
